item.title: Awami League flexes muscle in Gopalganj, DC, SP transferred
item.description:
Leaders and activists of the activities-banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations staged a major show of force in Gopalganj on Sunday, marching openly with sharp weapons, vandalising a police vehicle and public installations, and setting fire to the July Memorial, as the government transferred the district's deputy commissioner and superintendent of police following the unrest.
The processions, which continued from around 11am to 2pm, saw activists carrying machetes, axes, spears, sticks and oars through major streets of the district town, according to eyewitnesses and local reports.
Despite a heavy deployment of law enforcement personnel, the demonstrators marched through several areas, reopened the long-closed district Awami League office and damaged public property.
The unrest prompted the deployment of three additional platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), bringing the total to six platoons, comprising approximately 150 personnel.
Following the violence, Deputy Commissioner Md Arif-uz-Zaman was withdrawn and attached to the Ministry of Public Administration, while Habiganj DC GM Sarfaraz was appointed his replacement.
Superintendent of Police Md Habibullah was transferred to Feni, with Feni SP Pratyush Kumar Majumdar appointed to Gopalganj.
The transfers came amid questions over the authorities' response to the demonstrations, during which protesters were seen moving through the town despite the presence of police.
According to local sources, Awami League supporters began gathering at Ghosherchar Uttarpara in Latifpur union from around 8am.
One procession, reportedly led by municipal Awami League organising secretary Salauddin Khan, entered the town after crossing the BSCIC bridge.
Other groups, including one reportedly led by Chhatra League leader Md Samiul Haque and another by former councillor Al Amin, converged near the old launch terminal before heading towards the district Awami League office in Bankpara.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The demonstrators broke open the office, which had remained closed for an extended period, and celebrated its reopening.
Eyewitnesses said protesters vandalised and set fire to the July Memorial near the launch terminal.
They also removed the nameplate of Gopalganj Government College and displayed a banner identifying it as Government Bangabandhu College.
At Gopalganj University of Science and Technology, protesters damaged the nameplate at Hadi Chattar.
Several demonstrators climbed onto a police armoured personnel carrier, damaged its mirrors and spray-painted slogans supporting Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League.
A nearby police box was also vandalised.
Fires were lit on roads near the launch terminal, government college and press club, disrupting traffic.
Movement along the Gopalganj–Patgati road remained suspended for nearly three hours, according to local accounts.
At a press briefing, BGB Brigadier General Mahmud Hasan said the additional deployment was intended to maintain public safety and prevent further violence.
He said between 1,500 and 2,000 people, possibly more, had gathered around the deputy commissioner's office complex earlier in the day.
The BGB worked with other security agencies to restore calm, he added.
Dhaka Range DIG Md Mostafizur Rahman said approximately 1,350 police personnel had been deployed across Gopalganj, alongside BGB, Armed Police Battalion, Special Reserve Battalion and Ansar members.
He said security arrangements covered important government installations and a 67-kilometre stretch of the national highway, which remained operational.
However, eyewitness accounts described vandalism and road blockades in the district town, raising questions about the effectiveness of security arrangements.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
The unrest followed attacks on BNP and Jubo Dal offices in Tungipara on Saturday.
According to local witnesses and BNP leaders, Awami League and Chhatra League activists vandalised a Jubo Dal office at Barni Bazar before attacking and setting fire to a BNP office at Nilfa Bazar.
Several shops belonging to BNP supporters were also reportedly damaged.
Tungipara police OC Ayub Ali said police had received information about the incidents but no formal complaint had been lodged at the time.
The latest developments have renewed concerns about political violence in Gopalganj, where clashes surrounding an NCP rally in July 2025 resulted in four deaths.

item.title: BNP leaders’ properties vandalized, torched in Gopalganj
item.description:
Several homes, party offices and business establishments belonging to leaders and supporters of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and its affiliated organizations were vandalized and set on fire in Tungipara upazila of Gopalganj on Sunday.
BNP leaders alleged that activists of the banned Awami League, Jubo League and Chhatra League carried out the attacks in different areas of the upazila from Sunday afternoon, November 15.
According to local sources, Awami League and its affiliated organizations' activists brought out a procession at Pakurtia Bazar in Dumuria Union around 2pm. They later set fire to 2 business establishments belonging to BNP supporters beside Pakurtia Madrasa.
At around 3:30pm, another procession vandalized and set fire to the Jubo Dal office at Patgati Bazar.
At around 4pm, the attackers set fire to the house of Jasim Sheikh, former convener of the upazila Swechchhasebak Dal, in Sriramkandi.
At around 5pm, a shop belonging to BNP supporter Mahmud Biswas was set on fire at the Chowrangi intersection in Gawhardanga. Around the same time, a business establishment belonging to Abu Zafar Khan, organizational secretary of the municipal BNP, was vandalized at Tungipara Bazar.
Later, at around 8pm, the residence of Imdad Molla, president of the municipal BNP, at Patgati Bazar was vandalized and set on fire. The house of Gopal Sarkar, organizational secretary of the municipal BNP, was also vandalized around the same time.
At around 8:30pm, activists of the banned Chhatra League vandalized the house of Yen Munshi, convener of the municipal Chhatra Dal, in Patgati Madhyapara village.
Later, at around 9pm, a branch of Grameen Bank in Patgati, Tungipara, was set on fire.
Tungipara municipal BNP President Imdad Molla said: “Bangladesh is a democratic country. Everyone has the right to engage in politics here. Just because we are members of the BNP, will activists of banned organizations vandalize and burn down our homes? We demand punishment for those responsible.”
Earlier, on Saturday afternoon, November 14, activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organizations vandalized the office of Farid Gazi, joint convener of the upazila Jubo Dal, at Borni Bazar.
Later that night, the BNP office in Kushli Union was vandalized and set on fire.
Tungipara police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Ayub Ali said he had heard about incidents of vandalism and arson in different parts of the upazila since the afternoon.
However, he said no one had submitted a written complaint to the police station regarding the incidents.

item.title: Case filed against 53 AL men over alleged bomb attacks in Gopalganj
item.description:
A case has been filed under the Explosives Act against 28 leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations in Muksudpur, Gopalganj, over allegations of carrying out crude bomb attacks to create panic. Another 20 to 25 unidentified people have also been accused in the case.
Abdul Qaiyum Sharif, office secretary of the Muksudpur upazila BNP, filed the case with Muksudpur Police Station on Saturday afternoon. He is the son of Kamal Sharif of Tengrakhola village in the upazila.
Officer-in-Charge (OC) of the police station, Abdullah Al Mamun, confirmed the matter on Sunday afternoon.
According to the case statement, around 10pm on November 9, Abdul Qaiyum was returning home from Muksudpur Sadar when leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations allegedly exploded crude bombs in front of Muksudpur Government College to create panic as part of a nationwide programme announced by the party.
After receiving the information, a team of Muksudpur police rushed to the scene, prompting the accused to move towards Akij Jute Mills, located beside the Dhaka-Khulna highway.
The complainant followed them towards the mill. Later, when another police patrol team approached the area, the accused allegedly exploded another crude bomb near the entrance to Dasherhat Road, on the opposite side of the mill, before fleeing.
Following the incident, the case was filed on Saturday, naming 28 people and accusing another 20 to 25 unidentified individuals.
Confirming the case, OC Abdullah Al Mamun said the accused had allegedly exploded crude bombs in the name of enforcing a blockade programme, creating panic and terror among the public.
Police operations to arrest those accused are ongoing, he added.

item.title: SI hacked over Gopalganj police vehicle arson case
item.description:
A police sub-inspector who filed a case over the vandalism and arson of a police vehicle in Gopalganj's Tungipara has been hacked and injured by a group of people.
The incident took place near Chourangi intersection in Patgati union of Tungipara upazila on Sunday afternoon. The injured officer, SI Moslem Ali, is currently receiving treatment at Tungipara Upazila Health Complex.
Earlier, on Friday afternoon, Moslem Ali filed a case under the Anti-Terrorism Act, 2009, over the vandalism and arson attack on a police vehicle.
Police and local sources said leaders and activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations carried out widespread violence across Gopalganj on November 10.
From the morning, they reportedly took positions at several key locations in Tungipara with traditional weapons, including oars and sticks, and staged demonstrations and carried out vandalism and other violent activities.
At one point, attackers vandalised a police pickup van and set it on fire. Protesters also blocked different sections of the Gopalganj-Tungipara road by burning tyres, causing severe disruption to public movement.
Tungipara police station Officer-in-Charge Md Ayub Ali said a group of miscreants suddenly intercepted Moslem Ali's motorcycle and attacked him on Sunday afternoon.
He said the officer was rescued with the help of locals and taken to the upazila health complex for treatment.
The OC said those involved in the attack would be identified and legal action would be taken against them.
He added that the case filed over the police vehicle vandalism and arson named 2,224 accused, including 224 individuals and 2,000 unidentified people.
Meanwhile, local sources said leaders and activists of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations staged processions and rallies across Gopalganj on Sunday, carrying traditional weapons, including machetes, Chinese axes, spears and sticks.
During the demonstrations, a police armoured personnel carrier (APC) and a police box were vandalised. The protesters also damaged the nameplates of the July Memorial and Hadi Chattar.
The demonstrations were reportedly organised to make the November 19 lockdown program a success. Protesters broke through police barricades and marched along several roads in the town, while incidents of vandalism and arson were reported at different locations.
Panic spread across the town, forcing shops to close and disrupting normal movement.

item.title: Nusrat doubt she will get justice over alleged arson at ancestral home
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) lawmaker Nusrat Tabassum Joty on Sunday alleged that miscreants set fire to her family home in Kushtia and expressed doubt about the fairness of the investigation after the home minister's initial remarks on the incident.
Speaking in the House, the NCP MP said attackers set fire to her ancestral residence at Bagan village in Daulatpur upazila of Kushtia on the night of Thursday.
"I have been wounded twice in this arson attack. First, when I saw my home burnt down, and second, when I saw esteemed colleagues in this august House try to downplay the sabotage against my family," she said.
Citing CCTV footage, Joty said flames engulfed the house simultaneously, and women and children could be seen running out and collapsing, unconscious from the smoke.
She said an electric light on a wall of the house was still on at the time, which she described as clear visual evidence against claims that the house was abandoned or that the fire was caused by a short circuit.
She said the word "abandoned" was used at least five or six times in the House. She added that she was not aggrieved by the description of her home as such, but wondered how the fire could have been committed differently even if the house had been abandoned.
Joty said remarks by a senior official responsible for law and order during an ongoing investigation could influence the probe, as subordinates might feel tempted to prepare reports to please their superiors. She stressed that she was not saying this would happen, but said she had doubts about a fair investigation.
She also said the perpetrators had celebrated and claimed responsibility on social media and had threatened her, yet were being spoken of in terms of being forgiven.
She noted a similar pattern of arson in Gopalganj on Sunday, where, she said, offices of the BNP's student and youth wings, Chhatra Dal and Jubo Dal, were set on fire.
Demanding security for herself, her family and the frontline activists of the July uprising, Joty asked through the Speaker when and how she would get redress.
Responding, Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad said all members of the House had expressed sympathy for her. He said the home minister had told the House that the matter would be investigated and action taken, and had already asked the superintendent of police to visit the spot and directed other law enforcement agencies to ensure a proper probe.
"Let us see the result. You will get another opportunity once the report comes. Let the law enforcement agencies do their work now," the speaker told her.
He added that the apprehension of an affected person that an investigation could be influenced was not unparliamentary. He also expressed hope that the government and law enforcement agencies would take stern steps, since the home of a member of Parliament had been attacked.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed responding to the allegation against him said the fire broke out around 12:20am on Thursday in a house beside the Kushtia residence where Joty's parents live.
He said he spoke to the director general of the Fire Service and Civil Defence, the BGB director general and the district administration the following morning.
He said a probe committee had since been formed, headed by a deputy director of local government (DDLG). It includes a BGB officer of major rank, a police officer of assistant superintendent rank and an additional director of the Fire Service. The committee was given three days, with its term ending Sunday, and is due to submit its report Monday.
The minister said his earlier statement was based on preliminary findings, which had found no sign of petrol bombs. He said he had added that a short circuit could be possible, but had not made any conclusive remark. He maintained that the findings would be disclosed only after the investigation was complete.
Salahuddin said a goat had died in the fire and he had heard that cattle were also present. He acknowledged that people could have been in the house, saying he later saw video footage of a woman carrying a child out of the building. "All these will come under the investigation," he said.
He said Joty had filed a general diary (GD) and a case over the incident, and an investigation officer had been appointed for the case.
Regarding another GD she filed at Kalabagan police station on the same night over alleged threats by phone, he said the officer-in-charge could not yet provide details of the number used for the threats.
Objecting to Joty's remark that his statement could influence the investigation, the home minister said the expression should be expunged, as statements in the House are never made to influence any inquiry. He said any attack on a lawmaker or on lives and property would be dealt with strictly and without partisan consideration.

item.title: Two internet service provider employees shot in Rampura
item.description:
Two employees of an internet service provider were injured after a group of miscreants stormed its office and opened fire over an alleged Tk10 lakh extortion demand in Rampura, Dhaka, on Sunday evening.
The injured were identified as Saju Ahmed Rubel, 28, and Habib, 27. They were taken to the emergency department of Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH).
The incident occurred at the office of Speed Touch Network and Technology, beside Takwa Mosque on Wapda Road, around Sunday evening. Four to five young men entered the office and opened fire, leaving the two employees injured.
Habib said one of the attackers asked, “Why didn't you pay the money?” while another warned, “You cannot continue doing business here.” Two of the assailants were wearing masks and caps.
Bandon Kumar Saha, the company's network operations in-charge, said two individuals, identified as Guja Badsha and Jony, had demanded Tk10 lakh over the phone 15 to 20 days ago. They had also threatened to drive the company out of the area if the money was not paid.
Inspector Md Habibur Rahman, in-charge of the DMCH police outpost, said Rubel sustained a gunshot wound to his right leg, while Habib was shot in his left hand. Both were receiving treatment in the hospital's emergency department.
Habib is the son of Dulal Mia of North Matlab upazila in Chandpur, while Rubel is the son of Yusuf Mia of Nalchity upazila in Jhalakathi. Both lived at the company's office.
Rampura Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Jahangir Alam confirmed the incident, saying police were at the scene and investigating the matter.

item.title: Experts call for investment in follow-up care to prevent deaths of preterm newborns
item.description:
Health experts and policymakers have called for increased investment in post-discharge follow-up care, skilled healthcare professionals, neonatal facilities and integrated referral systems to reduce preventable deaths and long-term complications among premature and low-birth-weight newborns in Bangladesh.
The call came at a policy dialogue titled “Strengthening Care for Preterm and Low Birth Weight Newborns in Bangladesh” held in Dhaka on Sunday to mark World Prematurity Day 2026. The event was organised by UNICEF and Dhaka Tribune.
In his keynote presentation, Dr Dewan Md Emdadul Haque of UNICEF said Bangladesh records around 600,000 premature births annually out of 3.6–3.7 million total births. Nearly 67% of under-five deaths occur during the neonatal period, while prematurity and low birth weight account for an estimated 32% of under-five deaths.
He identified four major challenges to ensuring quality care: inadequate capacity in Special Care Newborn Units (SCANUs) and neonatal intensive care units (NICUs); limited respiratory support equipment, such as continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machines; weak referral and transportation systems; and shortages of trained staff, alongside difficulties in equipment maintenance.
He also noted that community-based Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) services remain limited to 10 intervention districts, while follow-up care for discharged newborns through the government's DHIS2 platform has yet to reach the desired level.
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), KMC is an evidence-based, life-saving method of caring for preterm and low-birth-weight newborns through continuous or frequent skin-to-skin contact and exclusive breastfeeding.
Dr Haque called for stronger antenatal care, improved maternal nutrition, expanded neonatal services and an integrated referral and post-discharge follow-up system connecting hospitals with community healthcare providers.
Participants at a policy dialogue to mark World Prematurity Day 2026, held in Dhaka on Sunday, November 15, 2026. Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
Around 16.2% of births in Bangladesh are premature, accounting for nearly 500,000 births annually. Complications associated with prematurity and low birth weight claim the lives of three newborns every hour.
Speakers stressed that saving premature babies' lives must be followed by sustained care after they leave hospitals, including regular health check-ups, nutritional support, growth monitoring and developmental assessments.
Dr Malalay Ahmadzai, chief of health (officiating and deputy representative) at UNICEF, said prematurity was not merely a healthcare issue but also a matter of development, human capital, equity and social justice.
She emphasised the need for government-led newborn services backed by sustainable public financing and government-managed information systems. She also called for stronger health systems and greater collaboration to ensure quality care throughout the continuum, from pregnancy to postnatal follow-up.
Dr Sharmin Sultana Urmi of Save the Children highlighted the need for an integrated neonatal referral and transportation system connecting public and private healthcare facilities.
She said an effective referral system required real-time information on hospital bed availability, facility readiness, trained personnel and properly equipped ambulances capable of transporting vulnerable newborns. Without better coordination, families often have to move between hospitals in search of available beds, delaying critical treatment.
Dhaka Tribune News Editor Anando Mostofa, who moderated the policy dialogue, said Bangladesh had made significant progress in maternal and newborn healthcare, but challenges remained in ensuring quality treatment, skilled staff, effective referrals and post-discharge follow-up.
He stressed that the goal should not be limited to saving premature newborns but should also include ensuring their healthy growth and development through sustained care.
Dr Ridwana Maher Manna, research investigator at the Maternal and Child Health Division of icddr,b, stressed the importance of linking hospital-based KMC with community healthcare services.
She suggested introducing digital reminders for scheduled follow-up visits, identifying the reasons for missed appointments and strengthening family-centred counselling to encourage parents to seek timely care.
Participants at a policy dialogue to mark World Prematurity Day 2026, held in Dhaka on Sunday, November 15, 2026. Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
She also referred to research conducted by icddr,b and Projahnmo Foundation, which highlighted the effectiveness of immediate KMC alongside special newborn care while identifying challenges related to bed capacity, space and infection prevention.
WHO's Dr Md Nurul Islam Khan called for a life-course approach to preventing premature births, beginning with adolescent health, nutrition and family planning and continuing through quality antenatal care and safe delivery.
He stressed the need to increase antenatal care coverage from four visits to eight, address the approximately 50% vacancy rate in the field-level health workforce and ensure dedicated personnel for newborn care. He also called for adequate budget allocations and clear administrative responsibilities for implementing and monitoring maternal and newborn health services.
Prof Dr Dilara Alo, professor of neonatology at the Centre for Medical Education in Dhaka, emphasised the need for investment in financial resources, skilled manpower and management.
She proposed establishing an online monitoring system to regularly collect data on newborn admissions, treatment outcomes and deaths, enabling policymakers to identify gaps and improve services.
Bangladesh has expanded KMC services from 57 facilities in 2018 to more than 460 in 2024. However, speakers said shortages of trained staff, inadequate equipment, limited specialised care and weak follow-up mechanisms continue to undermine progress.
They stressed that stronger investment and coordinated action are essential to achieving the Sustainable Development Goal target of reducing neonatal mortality to 12 deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030.

item.title: Mohammadpur pharmacy targeted with bombs, bullets over alleged extortion
item.description:
A pharmacy in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur has come under repeated crude bomb attacks and gunfire this month after its owner allegedly refused to pay Tk50 lakh in extortion money, raising fresh concerns over the activities of organised criminal gangs in the capital.
The latest attack occurred on Friday night, November 13, when unidentified assailants fired two shots at Anurag Pharma, opposite the National Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases, narrowly missing an employee.
Earlier, crude bombs were reportedly hurled at the establishment on November 5 and 7, leaving several passersby injured.
According to a complaint lodged with Mohammadpur police, the attacks followed an extortion demand made by individuals invoking the names of alleged gang leaders known as “Killer Badal” and “Killer Pappu.”
Pharmacy employee Moin Uddin said the threats began in early November when the criminals demanded Tk50 lakh from the owner.
As the money was not paid, the establishment came under repeated attacks, he alleged.
Describing Friday’s shooting, Moin said bullets shattered the shop’s glass, with one passing close to his head.
“We are currently living in a state of constant terror,” he said.
The owner also alleged that the extortionists had threatened to attack and burn down the establishment unless their demand was met.
Tejgaon Division Deputy Commissioner Ibn Mizan said multiple law enforcement units were working with local police to identify and arrest those responsible.
“We are working to apprehend this criminal group,” he said.
Additional Deputy Commissioner Md Jewel said investigators were examining CCTV footage to establish how the attacks occurred and identify the perpetrators.
Security has been strengthened in the area following the shooting.
Police have yet to publicly establish whether the suspects who demanded the money were directly linked to Badal or Pappu.
Anurag Pharma is part of a commercial establishment owned by Syed Hasan Nur Islam, also known as Rashton, a former city corporation councillor.
The building also houses a restaurant, a Chinese restaurant, a superstore and a telecom outlet.
According to the complaint, Nur Islam has remained in hiding since the fall of the Awami League government on August 5, 2024, although his businesses have continued operating.
The attackers allegedly targeted the establishment after their demand for extortion money was rejected.
Badal, widely referred to as “Killer Badal”, has long been associated with allegations of organised crime in Mohammadpur.
According to police records cited in the account, he faces numerous cases involving murder, extortion and illegal occupation of property.
Local sources allege that criminal groups operating under his name are involved in extorting businesses, controlling footpaths, drug trafficking and land grabbing.
Pappu and Lalu Uddin Lalu are among those identified by local sources as his associates.
However, investigators have not established their involvement in the pharmacy attacks.
The latest incidents have heightened anxiety among business owners and employees in Mohammadpur, where repeated threats and violent attacks have raised concerns about their safety.

item.title: Farmers demand climate justice, not debt at COP31
item.description:
Indigenous women farmers in the Barind region have demanded grant-based climate financing instead of loans, while coastal communities in Khulna have called for compensation from countries responsible for global warming, highlighting Bangladesh's growing demand for climate justice at the ongoing UN Climate Change Conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye.
The demands were raised at separate programmes in Rajshahi and Khulna on Sunday, calling for stronger international commitments to protect vulnerable communities from the impacts of climate change.
In Rajshahi, Indigenous women farmers from the Barind region urged developed countries to provide grants rather than loans to help vulnerable nations tackle climate-related losses.
They said climate adaptation financing for least developed countries (LDCs) must be entirely grant-based to prevent further debt burdens. They also demanded recognition and protection of the rights of women farmers, sharecroppers, agricultural workers, fishers and Indigenous communities.
The demands were raised at a gathering in Nabai Bottola village of Godagari upazila, organised under a nationwide campaign titled “From Field to Antalya: Farmers' Rights for a Just Transition”.
Around 30 civil society organisations are participating in the campaign to push for the protection of Bangladesh's agriculture sector and farmers' rights in COP31's final decisions.
Speakers, including Indigenous women leaders Kostanti Na Hansda and Sabitri Hembram, expressed disappointment over progress during the first week of the summit.
Citing a Carbon Brief analysis, they said new public climate finance commitments from developed countries had fallen by 71%, from around $40 billion annually to $11.7 billion. They also noted that a proposal to triple adaptation finance had not been included in the agenda.
According to the organisers, only 1.7% of global climate finance reaches smallholder farmers in developing countries. They said the $30 million in grants announced for Bangladesh at COP31 represented just 0.2% of the country's estimated annual climate-related losses of $15.2 billion.
The gathering urged COP31 leaders to adopt a permanent five-year programme on food and agriculture with dedicated funding and ensure farmers' and fishers' organisations have a formal role in climate negotiations.
Other demands included increasing renewable energy's share of electricity generation to at least 75%, releasing pledged climate compensation without delay, providing direct assistance to climate-affected farmers and cancelling unjust foreign debts. They also called for recognising agroecology as a solution to the climate crisis rather than relying on carbon markets.
The organisers urged the government to disclose details of the $30 million grant, ensure fair access to fertiliser and bring sharecroppers, women farmers, landless agricultural workers and fishers under farmer cards, crop insurance and social protection programmes.
Meanwhile, in Khulna, a symbolic boat-based human chain featuring empty earthen pitchers was held at Jailkhana Ghat, at the confluence of the Bhairab and Rupsha rivers, demanding climate justice, adequate financing for loss and damage, adaptation support and protection of coastal communities' rights.
The Climate Action Forum Khulna district committee organised the protest with support from the Local Environment Development and Agricultural Research Society (LEADERS), in connection with COP31.
Speakers said global warming and continued carbon emissions were driving sea-level rise, increasing salinity, river erosion, declining navigability, cyclones and tidal surges, threatening the lives and livelihoods of coastal communities.
They said people in Khulna, Satkhira and Bagerhat were facing growing shortages of safe drinking water, soil salinity, uncertain livelihoods and environmental degradation.
The speakers stressed that Bangladesh bears little responsibility for climate change but continues to suffer its devastating consequences. They demanded that countries responsible pay compensation to vulnerable nations, arguing that such payments should be treated as rightful claims rather than charity, loans or aid.
More than 50 people from different professions attended the Khulna programme. Empty pitchers, banners and placards displayed on the boats highlighted the drinking water crisis, salinity, river erosion and declining navigability affecting coastal communities.

item.title: 3 districts get new DCs
item.description:
The government has appointed new deputy commissioners (DCs) and district magistrates to Gopalganj, Chuadanga and Habiganj.
The Ministry of Public Administration issued separate notifications in this regard on Sunday.
According to the notifications, Habiganj DC Dr GM Sharfaraz has been transferred to Gopalganj as its new DC, while Gopalganj DC Md Arif-uz-Zaman has been attached to the Public Administration Ministry.
Deputy Secretary Md Alamgir Kabir of the Public Administration Ministry has been appointed as the new DC of Chuadanga. The district's outgoing DC, Lutfun Naher, has also been attached to the ministry.
Meanwhile, Cabinet Division Deputy Secretary Zakir Hossain has been appointed as the new DC of Habiganj.

item.title: SRB: No major security threats expected in December
item.description:
The Special Response Battalion (SRB) does not anticipate any major security threats in December and expects the country's law and order situation to remain normal.
SRB Legal and Media Wing Director Wing Commander MZM Intekhab Chowdhury said this at a press conference at the battalion's media centre in the capital's Karwan Bazar on Sunday.
“We do not anticipate any major threats surrounding December at this point. We are working alongside other law enforcement agencies and want to assure the people that the country's law and order situation will remain normal,” he said.
Asked how crude bombs were being brought into Dhaka despite police checkpoints, he said it was not possible to secure every part of the vast city, but law enforcement agencies were making every effort to maintain order.
On motorcycles allegedly used in recent crude bomb explosions, Intekhab Chowdhury said authorities were examining CCTV footage to identify those involved and had already made arrests.
He added that law enforcement agencies had stepped up searches of motorcyclists, their bags and other belongings at checkpoints to prevent sabotage.

item.title: Jubo Dal leader hacked to death over sand trade dispute in Mymensingh
item.description:
A Jubo Dal leader was hacked and stabbed to death allegedly by rivals over a dispute over control of the sand trade in Mymensingh city.
The deceased, Md Zaman, 35, was a member of the Jubo Dal's Ward 26 unit. He was the son of Abu Bakkar Siddique and a resident of the area.
The incident took place around 7pm on Sunday near Majid Market in Madhya Barera, a residential and commercial area under Ward 26 of Mymensingh City Corporation.
According to police and local sources, Zaman was riding his motorcycle to Barera Bazar with his young child on Sunday evening when several people, including local resident Mehedi Hasan, intercepted him near Majid Market. Before he could react, the attackers repeatedly stabbed him in the chest and hacked him with sharp weapons before fleeing the scene.
Locals rescued Zaman in critical condition and rushed him to the emergency department of Mymensingh Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
Zaman's elder brother, Roman Kawsar, who is also president of the Jubo Dal's Ward 26 unit, said Zaman had been involved in a dispute with another group of sand traders aligned with the Awami League over control of the local sand business. He alleged that the rival group had planned and carried out the killing over the dispute.
Mymensingh Additional Superintendent of Police Abdullah Al Mamun told Dhaka Tribune that the motive behind the killing had yet to be established.
"Several police teams are investigating the incident and trying to arrest those involved," he said.
The body has been kept at the morgue of Mymensingh Medical College Hospital for an autopsy.

item.title: Hridoy's century inspires Bangladesh's remarkable recovery against South Africa
item.description:
Towhid Hridoy struck a magnificent century as Bangladesh produced a remarkable recovery from 22-3 to finish the opening day of the first Test against South Africa at 327-6 at the Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg on Sunday.
Hridoy scored 137 before falling off the final delivery of the day, while Liton remained unbeaten on 92 to give Bangladesh a strong position heading into the second day.
The pair shared a record-breaking 206-run partnership for the sixth wicket, rescuing the visitors after Kagiso Rabada's devastating opening spell had threatened to derail their innings.
Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto won the toss and elected to bat, but the decision initially looked costly as Rabada struck with the very first delivery of the innings, dismissing Test debutant Mahfijul Islam Robin for a golden duck.
The South African pace spearhead then removed Mominul Haque and Shanto in quick succession, leaving Bangladesh reeling at 22-3 in the ninth over.
Tanzid Hasan Tamim and Hridoy subsequently steadied the innings with a 99-run fourth-wicket partnership. Tanzid made a valuable 67 before Rabada broke the stand after lunch, dismissing the opener and Mushfiqur Rahim off consecutive deliveries to reduce Bangladesh to 121-5.
However, Hridoy and Liton had other plans as they launched an impressive counterattack against the South African bowling attack.
Hridoy continued his remarkable run of form, following his unbeaten 242 against West Indies in Bangladesh's previous Test assignment just 10 days ago. His 137 in Johannesburg made him only the second Bangladesh batter to score a Test century against South Africa, after Mahmudul Hasan Joy in 2022.
The century was also his second in consecutive Tests, underlining his growing stature in the Bangladesh batting line-up.
Liton provided excellent support at the other end, combining patience with timely aggression to frustrate the home attack. He remained unbeaten on 92 at stumps and will resume on Monday just eight runs away from his century.
Their 206-run stand was the highest partnership by a Bangladesh pair against South Africa for any wicket, while the visitors also registered their highest-ever Test total against the Proteas.
Rabada was the standout bowler for the hosts, finishing with 5-51, but the rest of the South African attack struggled to provide support. Dane Paterson, Marco Jansen, Wiaan Mulder and Simon Harmer all went wicketless.
After being on the verge of a collapse in the morning, Bangladesh will head into the second day with renewed confidence, hoping Liton can complete his century and the lower order can further extend their impressive recovery.

item.title: Jamal questions tactics, Srabon apologises
item.description:
Bangladesh captain Jamal Bhuiyan has questioned the team's tactics, substitutions and management decisions following their heartbreaking 1-0 defeat to Pakistan in the SAFF Championship 2026 semi-final, while goalkeeper Mehedi Hasan Srabon has apologised to supporters for his costly mistake.
A late strike from Denmark-based winger Abdul Samad Shahzad in the 86th minute sent Pakistan into their first-ever SAFF Championship final, ending Bangladesh's hopes of reaching the title decider on home soil.
Srabon, whose unfortunate error contributed to the decisive goal, expressed his remorse in a Facebook post.
“I dreamed of celebrating with you all last night, not writing these words with a heavy heart.
“An unfortunate slip changed everything, and I know the disappointment it caused. I take this moment as a painful lesson. My sincere apologies to my teammates, coaches and every supporter.
“I'm truly Sorry, Bangladesh,” he wrote.
Jamal did not hide his frustration over Bangladesh's performance and the coaching staff's decisions, particularly the delay in introducing him as a substitute.
Speaking to journalists while leaving the team hotel, the midfielder revealed that the disappointment had kept him awake throughout the night.
“I feel terrible. I haven’t been able to sleep properly; I spent the entire night—until six in the morning—in Hamza’s room. I honestly expected to be brought on much earlier, but we only entered the field in the stoppage time. I spoke at length about this after the match. I was extremely angry,” Jamal said.
The Bangladesh captain also questioned the team's tactical approach, arguing that they failed to find a solution against Pakistan's five-man defensive line despite knowing what to expect.
“We didn’t play the way we did in the previous match,” Jamal noted. “One reason could be a tactical shortcoming. Did Pakistan bring something entirely new? We knew they would play with five defenders. Usually, there are specific strategies or solutions for facing a five-man defensive line, but we couldn’t find any in this match. It’s disappointing.”
Jamal further explained why he was unhappy with the timing of his introduction, saying he and two other substitutes had been asked to warm up much earlier but were only sent onto the pitch deep into stoppage time.
“Everyone on the team was exhausted by that point. I felt I should have been brought on sooner. Three of us were told to get ready in the 86th minute, yet we didn’t actually get onto the pitch until the second minute of stoppage time. I addressed this after the match; it’s only natural that I’d be angry. I don’t believe it was the right decision. But that’s life—at the end of the day, we lost and failed to reach the final,” he added.
The midfielder also suggested that the coaching staff should reflect on their team-management decisions, particularly the failure to rest key players during Bangladesh's previous group match against Sri Lanka.
Despite taking a 2-0 lead in that encounter, Bangladesh did not make the most of the opportunity to give some of their regular starters a rest ahead of the semi-final, which came just 48 hours later.
“After the match, the coach spoke to everyone in the dressing room. Several points have been raised. However, it is not just the players who need to learn; the management must learn as well,” Jamal said.
“In the previous match, when we were leading 2-0, we should have considered resting some key players. Every player is important, but someone like Hamza, for instance, needed a rest—especially since we had another match just 48 hours later. There were some errors there. Ultimately, though, the decision of who plays and who doesn’t rests with the coach.”
Bangladesh's semi-final exit has now left the team facing questions over their tactical execution and squad management, with Jamal's comments highlighting the frustration within the camp after a defeat that ended their hopes of lifting the trophy at home.

item.title: One blood, many names
item.description:
I read Ziauddin Choudhury’s Understanding the Modern Bangladeshi with the quiet gratitude one feels on hearing a stranger describe the inside of one’s own chest.
He traces, with a civil servant’s clarity, the long road by which a people learned to stop choosing: The rival answers to colonial India’s question -- the line that ran from Sir Syed to the Muslim League, minority and safeguards, against Bengal’s own instinct, which found identity in a language and a soil as much as in a faith.
He walks us through 1952, when “we are Muslims in Pakistan” quietly became “we are Bengalis whose tongue is our nationhood” and through 1971, which turned sentiment into a state.
He reads Article 12 of the 1972 Constitution as it was meant to be read -- not as an assault on religion, but as an assault on the use of religion as the ticket to power and citizenship. He ends, rightly, on Tagore and Nazrul. I would not change a word of it. I want only to sit beside him and add what a man sees from inside the thing he describes.
I am old enough to remember a Bangladesh that no constitution could legislate. In the first years after independence, in the lanes where I grew up, a friend had no religion. I do not mean we were tolerant of one another’s faiths; I mean the question did not arise.
I could not have told you, of half the boys I played with, whether their mothers turned toward Mecca or lit a lamp before an image -- it was not a thing one knew, because it was not a thing that mattered.
That society was real. I did not dream it. And the slow tearing of that fabric, thread by thread, in the decades since, is a wound those of us who remember carry still. I write, in part, to describe the wholeness before it is forgotten by those too young to have stood in it.
For I was born beside a Bengali river, into a family that would be called Hindu, though I have never once been able to feel the border that word is meant to draw around me. I am not a theologian. I am, if anything, a civilizational Sanatani -- heir to an old subcontinental inheritance the way a Florentine is heir to the Renaissance, not by doctrine but by blood and weather and song.
My DNA is the DNA of the subcontinent, which is to say it is Hindu and Muslim and Buddhist and a dozen older things at once, and it has never asked me to choose. So when Ziauddin Choudhury writes that being Bengali and being Muslim need not negate each other, I do not read it as a Muslim’s reassurance. I read it as the description of my own body.
And let me grant, plainly, what a man with my name is not always expected to grant. Some time ago I sat reading the old constitutional quarrel of the 1930s -- Jinnah insisting that the Muslims of India needed a voice of their own, one the Hindu majority could not simply overrule; Nehru, the secular, unable to see how faith could enter a question of constituencies at all. It was an all-India argument, about Hindus and Muslims in the abstract; neither man had Bengal in his thoughts, and the word Bengali appears nowhere in it. But as I read, my mind slipped homeward, to my own soil, and a sentence rose in me -- not a proverb, nothing I had been taught, only my own voice murmuring what I suddenly understood: Musolmanra to jole bheshe aseni -- the Muslims did not come floating down the river.
The Bengali Muslim is no stranger washed in from elsewhere. Some came to Islam by conversion and many did not; but all of them rose from this very soil, the same villages, and the same rivers that gave me my grandfathers.
The Bengali Muslim and the Bengali Hindu are not two peoples who learned to share a country. They are one people wearing two of its names. This is not a poet’s flourish: Their belonging is not a courtesy I extend, but a fact older than any objection could be.
Let me give the synthesis a face, from the side Choudhury was too modest to claim. In the house where I grew up, the morning did not begin with a clock. It began with the Azan from the mosque down the lane, and it was by that call -- a Muslim call, in a Hindu household -- that my mother knew the hour to wake her son for his studies.
No one found this strange. The Azan was not another faith intruding; it was the sound of morning itself, the texture of a shared Bengali dawn. We were not tolerated guests at the edge of the nation. We were the nation, in one of its oldest forms.
Let me confess something that may surprise anyone who reads only the name at the top of this essay. I do not pray to Durga. And yet few sights give me more joy than a Bengali home at Diwali -- the rows of small lamps along the windowsills and the rooftops, the whole simple, childlike happiness of a festival of light that now glows from Dhaka to Kolkata to New York.
The only thing that moves me as much is the sight of children in their new clothes on Eid morning, shining with a pride they can barely hold in. I love both the same, and for the same reason.
To me, neither is theology; both are culture -- the way a people’s faith flowers into everyday life -- and such culture is among the most beautiful things human beings have ever made. A man who can be stirred by the Azan, light a lamp at Diwali, and smile at an Eid procession has not lost his religion. He has understood what religion was for.
This is why the minority is not a footnote to the story of modern Bangladesh. It is the proof of the story. A secularism that forbids religion from deciding citizenship is only as true as its weakest-placed citizen.
Choudhury notes, almost in passing, the great Hindu departure from East Bengal, and maps the longing for undivided Bengal onto the Hindus of the western shore -- those who left. But the leaving and the staying were often one family, not two.
My own parents and grandparents did not go. Yet most of my kin did -- nearly all of my mother’s people, nearly all of the family I married into -- packing in a single season what it had taken generations to root.
So I do not write as one who stayed, gazing across at those who left. I write from the torn seam itself, where half a household remained and half became a memory on the far side of a line.
For those of us on the staying side, East Bengal is not the recollection of a lost ancestral home across a border. It is home -- and we are what remains of the synthesis here, keeping it because someone must.
In the summer of 2024 and the months that followed, temples were burned and homes were marked; and last month -- in an image I cannot forget -- a mural of Rabindranath Tagore in Dhaka was defaced, blackened, as if the Bishwakobi himself, the first of all Asia to win the Nobel, could be painted out of the place that raised him.
When a mob blackens Tagore, it is not a Hindu who is attacked. It is the synthesis. It is the very thing Choudhury spent his essay defending. For Tagore belongs to no sect; he belongs to the morning, like the Azan.
And here the oldest lesson returns to warn us. A people cannot bury their language in the grave of their faith; when they are forced to, the nation tears. East Pakistan was Muslim -- as Muslim as the West -- and it tore anyway -- first in spirit, in 1952, when its students died for their mother tongue, and then in body, in 1971 -- because identity is never one thread, and you cannot pull out the thread of language in the name of the thread of religion without the whole cloth coming apart in your hands.
That is not a Hindu’s grievance nor a Muslim’s. It is simply what our history taught us. We learned it once, against an imposed tongue. We must not now unlearn it against one another.
Consider Nazrul, whom Choudhury rightly names in the same breath as Tagore. Our rebel poet wrote hamds and naats to the Prophet with one hand and shyama sangeet to the goddess Kali with the other; he married across the very line that was meant to be uncrossable, and raised children who carried both inheritances in their names.
Nazrul was not a Muslim poet who dabbled, nor a secular poet who hedged. He was the non-divide itself, walking around in a single body, singing. If we wish to know what the modern Bangladeshi could be, we need no constitutional theory. We need only read him.
I am not writing as a Hindu, pleading a Hindu’s case. I am writing for everyone this ancient and exhausting divide has ever wounded -- the Muslim woman told her Bengali songs are un-Islamic; the Hindu shopkeeper watching his shutter; the Buddhist in the Chittagong Hills, the Christian in the north; and the Bengali Muslim majority too, robbed of something each time a zealot insists their faith can be purchased only at the price of their culture.
The wound has no religion. That is the whole point. It cuts through one body -- ours -- and the blood that runs from it is one blood, whatever name we give it.
Choudhury ends on a hope: A Bangladesh where one may love Tagore, keep Pohela Baishakh, and hold Islam close, with no identity forced to negate another. I share that hope entirely.
I would only extend it by a single clause. The synthesis is complete not when no Bengali must choose between being Bengali and being Muslim -- that is already won, and Choudhury has shown us how.
It is complete when no Bengali must disappear to let another feel whole. A nation does not prove its secularism by the comfort of its majority. It proves it at the temple that is not burned, the mural that is not blackened, the neighbour whose morning prayer -- to whatever name, in whatever tongue -- is simply allowed to be the sound of the street.
Rajani K Saha writes from Stockholm, Sweden, where he has practised medicine for a lifetime, and where, on winter mornings, he sometimes still wakes up expecting an Azan that is five thousand kilometres away.

item.title: Is China expanding its military presence in Southeast Asia?
item.description:
It’s often said that maintaining good relations with your neighbors is essential. So in early November, China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi invited his counterparts from Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Thailand and Myanmar to Beijing.
There the six countries agreed on closer economic and security cooperation.
The visit is just one example of China’s growing influence on Southeast Asia. It’s not just about trade or infrastructure either, it’s also increasingly about military cooperation.
For instance, at the end of September, China and Laos opened a joint military support and training center north of the Laotian capital, Vientiane. Initially Laotian air force pilots are to be trained at the Ban Keun airfield, China has said.
Earlier in 2025 China expanded its footprint at Cambodia’s Ream naval base. China uses the facility on the Gulf of Thailand for logistics and training. And while Japanese and Vietnamese ships can visit the port, they’re docked at a southern quay and it’s unclear if other navies can use the same facilities under the same conditions as China.
“It remains to be seen how this [Ban Keun] will change China’s military access to Southeast Asia,” says Marco Bünte, a professor of Asian politics at the University Erlangen Nuremberg in Germany.
In recent years, China has significantly expanded its economic influence in the region.
The China-Laos railway and other infrastructure projects connect Laos more closely with its northern neighbor. Laos is also heavily indebted to China.
Bünte points out that Laos and Cambodia have been close military partners of China for some time and the new facility in Laos can be seen as another step towards deepening cooperation.
If that proves correct, “China would gain strategic depth in mainland Southeast Asia,” Bünte explained. “It would also give China better military access to the South China Sea.”
Johann Fuhrmann, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation’s Beijing office, points out that one should distinguish between training Laotian pilots and any potential use of the facilities by Chinese armed forces later.
“China gains influence when it co-designs the training and operation of such facilities over several years,” Fuhrmann told DW.
But nobody should underestimate China’s military positioning, Bünte continued. “China is expanding its military operational capabilities here although I wouldn’t speak of military hegemony because China hasn’t achieved that yet.”
With regard to the Laotian airbase, China says that Laotian pilots will be trained there. But beside military transporters and helicopters, Laos actually only has three light combat aircraft by Russia’s Yakovlev works.
According to the aviation media outlet FlightGlobal, four more K-8s, Chinese two-seat intermediate jet trainer and light attack aircrafts, are in service there. Satellite images analyzed by the Reuters news agency in early October show eight K-8s at the base — even thought this doesn’t necessarily mean they are stationed there permanently.
Fuhrmann doesn’t think anybody should jump to conclusions about this.
“The idea of ​​a Chinese air corridor is more of a future scenario than something that has already been proven,” he says.
For example, the runway at Ban Keun is only 2,000 meters (6,562 feet) long, which makes it too short for large Chinese bombers. These usually require 3,000 meters.
The crucial question is what rights China will be granted, Fuhrmann continues: “Will China have to obtain the approval of the respective government for every new use? Or are there longer-term commitments that both sides can invoke, even in times of crisis?”
Surrounding countries are reacting differently to what appears to be China’s growing influence in Laos, Cambodia and Myanmar because these countries are already considered closer to China.
Other Southeast Asian nations are hedging, trying to expand their relationship with China without severing ties with the US and also maintaining economic links with other Western nations. China’s involvement offers them additional options and Beijing wants to explore those possibilities. That’s just pragmatic though, Bünte says of the smaller Asian nations.
“Overall, these states… try to keep as many options open as possible,” he notes.
Vietnam and the Philippines are watching developments particularly closely. Both have territorial disputes with China in the South China Sea. But Vietnam also has close historical ties to Laos and trained its own military there.
In early November, the Vietnamese government declared that any military cooperation must serve peace and stability and referred to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia, commonly known as the Asean Treaty. China is not an Asean member but has also stated that its activities are not directed against any third parties.
“So far, these are individual steps,” Bünte adds. “We would have to wait and see if this leads to a broader military alliance in the years to come.”
Fuhrmann says that Western nations should help strengthen the smaller countries in the region and take their interests seriously.
“Ultimately, a counterweight can only be achieved through tangible contributions, not through warnings or lectures from Europe,” he says.

item.title: AIUB signs MoU with Indonesia’s Telkom University
item.description:
American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB) has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Indonesia’s Telkom University to strengthen cooperation in education, research, community service and institutional development, while expanding international academic ties between the 2 institutions.
Dr Carmen Z Lamagna, a member of AIUB's board of trustees, signed on behalf of AIUB. Professor Dr Suyanto, rector of Telkom University, signed on behalf of his institution.
Senior officials from both institutions were present at the signing ceremony.
The agreement establishes a framework for academic and institutional cooperation between the 2 universities. Under the partnership, the institutions will work together to expand mutual engagement in education and research, conduct joint research activities, collaborate on community service and social welfare initiatives, and strengthen institutional capacity and resources.
Through the partnership, AIUB and Telkom University will also exchange knowledge, experience and expertise while exploring new areas of future collaboration.
The agreement is expected to expand opportunities for international academic engagement and cooperation for students and teachers of both institutions.
The signing is part of AIUB's ongoing efforts to expand its international academic network through partnerships with reputed universities across the world and establish meaningful institutional collaborations.

item.title: Folk identity on Shakoor’s canvas
item.description:
Culture and heritage serve to express our identity, as well as that of the artists dedicated to reviving our folk and traditional arts.
Abdus Shakoor Shah is one such artist, widely acknowledged for his folk motifs and ballads. Throughout his extensive career, Shakoor has focused on folk motifs and ancient ballads.
The folk ballads of Mymensingh, including the renowned love stories of Mahua and Malua, Nakshi Kanthar Maath, Gazir Pata, and Manasha Pata, have been prominently featured in his paintings. In his artworks, he outstandingly displays peacocks and parrots. Additionally, Shakoor incorporates various animals such as elephants, bulls, dogs, cats, tigers, birds, serpents, and reptiles, all serving as delightful and decorative motifs.
Different kinds of fish and floral representations are also incorporated into his creations.
A significant number of his artworks focus on the themes surrounding Bangladeshi village women, encompassing their love stories, tragedies, aspirations, anxieties, and narratives of daily existence infused with romantic creativity. The pieces, characterised by a dominance of black and brown hues, alongside striking vermilion and gold, harmonise with shades of blue and green. Additionally, Shakoor incorporates elements such as flowers, birds, animals, and reptiles, including lizards and venomous snakes.
cover (1)
Abdus Shakoor Shah was born in 1946 in Bogura. He was immersed in its vibrant cultural environment and stunning natural scenery as he grew up. He took great pleasure in traditional fairs and religious celebrations, including puja and Moharram, along with the lively atmosphere that accompanied them. The colour patterns and designs of traditional dolls, artifacts, and household items consistently captivated him. He believed these influences were somehow embedded in him since his childhood.
Shakoor obtained his primary and secondary education from the local school situated in his village. He completed his Intermediate at Government Azizul Haque College in Bogura. In 1965, he was admitted to East Pakistan College of Arts and Crafts, which is now known as the Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Dhaka. He earned his Bachelor of Fine Arts (BFA) degree in the Drawing and Painting Department in 1970.
Subsequently, he took on the role of a lecturer at Sylhet Residential Model College, currently referred to as Sylhet Cadet College. In 1976, Shakoor became a lecturer at the Government Teachers' Training College in Chittagong.
That same year, he was awarded the Indian Government Scholarship to pursue a postgraduate diploma in mural design at MS University in Baroda, India. While there, he became involved with the Revivalist Group, which sought to rejuvenate the tradition of indigenous and ethnic art. During this period, he participated in exhibitions at the Bombay Art Society, Gujarat Lalit Kala Academy, and Baroda Municipal Corporation.
In 1977, he became the first Bangladeshi artist to receive the Gujarat Lalit Kala Academy Award. Throughout this time, he explored various mediums, including sand casting, tapestry, relief work, fresco, and tempera.
cover
After returning from Baroda in 1978, Shakoor engaged in abstraction for a period. During this phase of his career, he focused on themes such as inequality, political hypocrisy, deceit, and debauchery within society. He discovered that abstract patterns were a fitting medium for expressing his indignation. Additionally, he aimed to illustrate the pain and suffering experienced by people through his depictions of broken huts and shattered windows.
However, it was primarily through the use of colour that he sought to convey the distress of these individuals. Regrettably, both critics and his fellow artists appeared to show little interest in his work during that time.
During that time, Shakoor also re-entered the Government Teachers' Training College in Chittagong. In 1980, he made a transfer to the Bangladesh Government College of Arts and Crafts (presently the Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Dhaka) to serve as a lecturer.
The Craft Department of Fine Arts underwent modifications and modernisation under Shakoor's influence. He instructed students in hand weaving, sand casting, and fresco techniques.
Before the 1990s, Shakoor focused on various subjects, including pure abstraction, semi-abstraction, issues related to the Third World, the Liberation War, and malaria. However, he felt unable to express his thoughts adequately. Unexpectedly, he discovered a new subject of interest.
He encountered a Shital Pati in the Ceramics Department, where he was confronted by various animal forms, particularly the tiger and peacock. In 1991, Japan hosted an open art competition in which Shakoor took part. He created drawings featuring tigers and peacocks adorned with folk motifs.
He submitted these artworks to Japan, which were subsequently selected for an award. He was honoured to receive the award from Japan.
This marked the beginning of his exploration into folk art. He embraced folk art as a means of both sustenance and survival. Through folk art, he has discovered the strength to restore his self-belief and redefine his artistic language. He is relishing his engagement with folk and indigenous art. He sees no reason to depart from this path in search of new sources of inspiration. He is committed to experimentation and believes that his exploration of the folk domain is far from complete. His artistic ambition is to elevate folk designs and patterns to even greater heights within the realm of fine art.
cover (2)
Shakoor now believes that his critics provided him with a significant benefit by evaluating his initial endeavors.
During that time, he felt sad and isolated. He sought out new forms of artistic expression. He committed to avoiding following the paths of established artists and began exploring folk museums in both Bangladesh and Kolkata. Additionally, he made extensive visits to the Gurusaday Museum in Kolkata.
This museum boasts a remarkable collection of around 3,300 stunning exhibits of folk arts and crafts, which vividly showcase the energy and essence of rural life while also illustrating the art, social traditions, religious beliefs, practices, and motifs, along with aesthetic integration and cultural influences.
At a certain time, Shakoor reconnected with the works of Jamini Roy and became deeply absorbed in them for a period. Quamrul Hasan was also a significant source of inspiration for him. Evaluating the creations of established artists confirmed to him that he was progressing in the correct direction. Their influence uplifted his spirits. He began to understand that it was feasible to steer his art away from the confines of Western modernism. Fragments of images from his childhood memories, filled with the colors of the world and patterns of folk artifacts, started to resurface. Before long, he found himself mentally ready to explore new realms of expression.
Shakoor's artwork transcends mere illustrations of traditional ballads. He stylistically incorporates calligraphy onto his canvas, often featuring human figures alongside birds and animals. Each piece conveys a complete narrative that conceals our identity.
In certain paintings, creatures such as birds, snakes, and elephants are depicted. The presence of tigers and a centrally placed elephant highlights the beauty of rural landscapes, where birds, flowers, cattle, and snakes harmoniously blend to form a stunning natural tableau.
The paintings possess a primitive essence while simultaneously exhibiting modern execution. The lines employed are not necessarily stylised; rather, they reflect a child's interactive spirit with bold outlines. The treatment of these lines is straightforward and unrefined, providing an authentic illustrative quality to the artworks as a whole. The artist typically works with four mediums: ink-drawing, opaque watercolor, acrylic, and oil. Among these, he predominantly favors 'opaque-watercolor' and acrylic, having also utilized gouache in a series of his works.
Shakoor consistently incorporates new elements (including the stitch work of traditional quilts created by village women and the characteristics of alpana) to enhance their visual attractiveness.
The edges of the compositions display a vibrant, repetitive pattern reminiscent of traditional scroll paintings (such as Gazir Pata or Manshar Pata). He employs flat, earthy tones alongside vivid colors to highlight the contrast between romance and reality, as well as life and death. The majority of Shakoor's current work
exhibit this reimagined style.
. cover (4)
Shakoor believes that he endeavours to represent his country through his artwork. When his pieces are exhibited in various galleries around the world, any foreign observer can easily recognise that these paintings originate from this sub-continent.
His aim is to ensure that any viewer can glance at his work and immediately identify that these scenes depict Bangladesh. His primary colours are blue, black, and red, which impart a meditative quality to the characters, outlined by black and white lines against vibrant backgrounds.
The treatment of his figures in some paintings, bordered by delicate black lines, is rich in gestures and emotions, evoking a sense of ancient scripture in his art. His ink drawings are executed in contour, with a sense of space in the background, which lends the composition a resemblance to portraits.
Through Shakoor's dynamic brushstrokes and malleable textures, the canvas acquires a lively and energetic appearance. He has achieved a mysterious quality in his paintings that resonates on multiple levels, from the visual to the subconscious. A critical examination of his works evokes the impression that his acrylic mimics the typical tonalities of watercolors – gentle and seemingly translucent. Tranquility serves as a crucial element in Shakoor's creations. The subjects depicted in his works convey a sense of melancholy, which is consistently emphasised. The interaction of light and shadow has been exceptionally highlighted in his pieces.
Shakoor's artworks showcase a celebration of triumph and expansive vision. He derives joy from painting what inspires his creative spirit, allowing him to convey a personal language through colours and figurative representations. His themes consistently honour the magnificence of life. In this process, the audience also gains insight into the artist's unique personality and emotional state.
cover (3)
Space holds immense importance in Shakoor's artwork, serving as the primary allure of his creations. He possesses a remarkable talent for depicting mass, volume, and texture, while also crafting sensitive and exceptional compositions. For art enthusiasts, his paintings offer a fresh and captivating aesthetic, granting viewers a profound sense of enjoyment. His works are vibrant representations of his thorough exploration of the subjects he portrays. His drawings and sketches are animated and reveal an appropriate level of restraint.
Shakoor consistently selects a specific language to convey the narratives behind his paintings vividly. He has been passionately examining the movements of figures and the organisation of objects for an extended period. In this regard, the artist exercises great care in his objects and the arrangement of figures.
Shakoor embodies both a workaholic nature and a scholarly approach. Throughout the years, he has persistently engaged in experimentation. His detailed descriptions of various animal forms and human figures impart a fresh significance to his artworks. Each of his exhibitions showcases a unique perspective. The artist is consistently motivated to discover new concepts. This pursuit alleviates monotony for him, and he holds the belief that art can be enhanced through innovative experimentation.
Abdus Shakoor has been honoured with several accolades, which stand as clear evidence of his remarkable abilities. He has garnered several national and international awards, such as the Best Prize at the Lalit Kala Akademi in Gujarat in 1977, the Excellence Award in Tokyo, Japan in 1991, the Runner-up Prize at the International Noma Concours (ACCU) Competition in Tokyo in 2000, the Sultan Award in Bangladesh, as well as the Honourable Award and Gold Medal for the National Exhibition in Bangladesh.
He was also awarded the Civitella Ranieri Fellowships in Italy and received the Diploma Certificate from the Poland Print Biennial. Shakoor has held sixteen solo exhibitions and has participated in over one hundred and fifty group exhibitions both domestically and internationally, including in the USA, England, Poland, Argentina, Japan, France, China, Iran, Panama, Italy, and India.
Abdus Shakoor is fortunate to have a son and a daughter, along with a grandson and a granddaughter.
Takir Hossain is an art critic and cultural curator.
