Leaders of the Sylhet District Bus, Minibus, Coach and Microbus Workers' Union withdrew the strike at 9pm on Sunday after a meeting at the office of the Sylhet Metropolitan Police Commissioner at his request.
Moinul Islam, president of the union, confirmed the decision at 10:45pm.
Earlier, the strike was announced at a meeting held at the union office in Babna Point, South Surma, on Saturday afternoon under the banner of the Sylhet District Road Transport Owners and Workers Coordination Council.
The workers had called the strike to press three demands.
These include the withdrawal of cases filed against workers' leaders over the deaths of two workers at Kadamtali Terminal; the allocation of designated parking spaces for auto-rickshaws, easy-bikes, legunas and microbuses, alongside the removal of battery-run rickshaws, easy-bikes and tomtoms from the city; and the provision of bank challan numbers for CNG-run auto-rickshaws.

item.title: Is it the technology or its owners?
item.description:
Sixty years ago, the idea of everyone having a video phone in their pocket was the stuff of science fiction.
That people might spend more time on devices doing things other than making actual phone calls would have seemed stranger still, but here we are. A world where fretting about the impact of our own and other peoples’ screen time on society is a more likely choice to make than going without a phone.
As with climate change, individual decisions and consumer choices count enough to make a difference, but most of the actual power to substantively improve regulations and standards rests with politicians and giant global corporations.
In the run-up to the US mid-term Congressional elections this month, Silicon Valley companies and their owners donated $600 million dollars to Republican candidates.
A large proportion of this came from Elon Musk spending about $200m on supporting Ken Paxton, the losing Republican candidate for a Senate seat in Texas.
Whilst the vast amounts given to Republican candidates did not prevent an anti-Trump wave of Democratic party successes, they reflect the growing amounts being spent by Silicon Valley titans on buying political influence.
Big Tech’s societal and environmental footprint and its record of abusing monopolistic positions, aggressively minimizing paying taxes, failing to safeguard privacy, and designing algorithms to addict users and profit from amplifying political extremes and other harmful content already raises many ethical questions. Yet, the latest spending added to the concerns about its political lobbying and future trajectory.
Moore’s law, named after a co-founder of Intel, observed that the number of transistors it is technically possible to fit onto an integrated circuit can be doubled every two years at little increase in cost. For decades it was this rate of exponential improvement that enabled ever more computing power to be made available at lower prices to ordinary consumers.
In turn, these underpinned bigger projections and valuations for the sector. In 2016, the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization was Apple with the aggregate value of its shares peaking above $500bn.
Ten years on, its value is ten times larger at $5 trillion. This is different from being the world’s largest company by actual revenue; Apple’s revenues place it as only the seventh largest company.
Apple’s stock market value reflects the willingness of investors to bet on the tech sector’s future growth. Since 2020 this optimism has become based less on Moore’s law delivering cost reductions for consumers -- its effect is slowing down as semiconductor manufacturers adjust to the growing complexity and cost of making ever smaller circuits just as global supply chains have fragmented -- and more on a belief in future profits from AI.
Potential impacts of AI, both positive and negative, are easy enough to imagine, given the pace of change the sector is promising. Predictions of technological dystopias and utopias are a hardy staple of speculative fiction.
Right now, AI has an insatiable appetite for capital investment in scaling up computational power and data centres. These are demanding ever greater amounts of electricity and water for cooling systems.
The cost neutral arithmetic of energy costs remaining stable as computer chips and systems become smaller and more powerful promised by Moore’s law has been turned completely upside down by a globalized gold rush to grow AI.
Even in a world that had free energy, this direction of travel would be controversial given the sector’s impact on jobs, but in a world with a growing population seeking to cut carbon emissions, amid plenty of pre-existing concerns about Big Tech, it is politically toxic.
Seen in this light, the sectors’ growing political donations and lobbying efforts on AI, not just in the United States, but in countries around the world, are easy to explain.
Like other industries, it wants to keep pipelines of investment flowing and persuade politicians to support them with financial incentives and favourable laws.
But what if it is all just snake oil and a digital Ponzi scheme?
Scepticism is a rational stance given the vast scope and impact of the IT sector. But even where politicians seek to regulate aspects of the sector, their actions tend to be limited or seem like locking a stable door after the horse has bolted.
Given that parts of the sector like digital cryptocurrencies were designed to be largely decentralized and unregulated in nature, such naivete is troubling given that aspects of it can be used to enable criminality.
Dogmatic faith in future growth and cultish attitudes towards IT founders and products abound around the sector and among many consumers. Perhaps not surprisingly, many of the biggest critics of the ownership structures and strategies of the sector come from within its highly educated workforce and support the open-source movement.
Of course, the argument that technology is simply a tool that can be used for good or bad is ostensibly an objective one.
But when those making it are tech giants with monopolistic tendencies that stand to profit either way, calls for democratic scrutiny, breaking up monopolies, public accountability, and for that matter public ownership, all deserve to be heard.
It’s the oligarchs, stupid.
Niaz Alam is London Bureau Chief, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Dhaka air 3rd worst in world Monday morning
item.description:
Dhaka's air quality remained ‘very unhealthy’ on Monday morning, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 208 at 9:10am.
With this score, the capital ranked third among the world's most polluted cities.
A ‘very unhealthy’ air quality level means people, regardless of their health condition, may experience more serious health effects from air pollution. Even short-term exposure can affect anyone.
Pakistan's Lahore topped the list with an AQI score of 306, followed by India's Kolkata with 255.
Earlier, at 8:30am on Sunday, Dhaka also ranked third among the world's most polluted cities, with an AQI score of 206.
According to the AQI scale, readings of 101-150 are considered unhealthy for sensitive groups, while scores of 151-200 indicate unhealthy air quality. Readings of 201-300 are classified as very unhealthy, while scores above 300 are considered hazardous and pose serious health risks.
The AQI measures daily air quality, indicating pollution levels and their potential effects on public health.
In Bangladesh, air quality is assessed based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths worldwide each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Calling out the digital inquisitors
item.description:
In the interconnected landscape of modern South Asia, the digital square was once heralded as a beacon of democratic expression. Today, however, it increasingly resembles a medieval plaza where a baying mob gathers, stones in hand, waiting for the next target to be dragged into the light.
Across India, Pakistan, and the wider region, whenever tragedy strikes or a viral controversy erupts, a familiar and sickening ritual unfolds online. Behind a shroud of anonymous handles, inactive profile pictures, and automated bot networks, a pervasive strain of digital chauvinism rears its head.
These faceless commentators rush with predatory speed to demean, judge, and ultimately blame women for their own suffering.
Whether it is a high-profile criminal case of rape and murder, a domestic abuse tragedy, or a viral public misstep, the verdict from this digital jury is always preemptive and predictable: The woman is guilty.
This phenomenon is not merely an annoyance of modern internet culture; it is a profound social rot.
It reveals a deep-seated, short-sighted misogyny that weaponizes human suffering to reinforce archaic prejudices, demanding that we confront and socially shun these insidious behaviours before they erode the moral fabric of our societies.
The anatomy of victim-blaming
The most harrowing manifestation of this online malice occurs in the wake of heinous crimes -- rapes, assaults, and murders that shock the public conscience.
In a just society, a horrific crime against a woman should provoke universal outrage, sorrow, and an uncompromising demand for justice against the perpetrator.
Yet, in the virtual echo chambers of South Asia, the narrative is routinely subverted.
When a woman is attacked or killed, the digital inquisitors immediately pivot away from the perpetrator’s guilt to dissect the victim’s life with microscopic scrutiny.
Why was she out alone at night? Where was her male guardian or family member? What was she wearing?
In cases involving minors, the depravity sinks even lower, with commentators bizarrely projecting adult anxieties onto children, questioning their clothing or presence in public spaces as if to rationalize the unrationalizable.
This is the quintessence of victim-blaming. It is a psychological defense mechanism rooted in a fragile worldview that cannot bear the thought of a chaotic, dangerous world where women are independent agents.
By blaming the victim, these commentators construct a comforting illusion of control: “If she hadn’t done X, Y, or Z, she would have been safe.”
In doing so, they absolve the actual criminal and place the burden of virtue and safety entirely on the shoulders of women.
It sends a chilling message to half the population: Your safety is conditional, and if you step outside the narrow parameters dictated by society, your tragedy is your own fault.
Attire, liberty, and the ‘liberal mind’
Beyond violent crimes, everyday viral controversies draw the same predatory swarm.
Let a video surface of a woman making a mistake in public, navigating a personal dispute, or simply living her life on her own terms, and the social media comment sections transform into cesspools of moral panic.
Here, the faceless profiles deploy a standard checklist of grievances.
Every complex socio-economic issue, every cultural shift, and every personal failure is summarily blamed on "indecent attire," "polygamous behaviour" (often invoked as a catch-all insult), and the dreaded "liberal mind."
If a woman exercises agency over her life, her career, or her relationships, she is immediately branded as a corrupting influence on traditional values.
The underlying rhetoric is transparently hypocritical: Men can indulge in every conceivable excess without denting their moral standing, but a woman’s entire character is judged by a single snapshot, a rumour, or a manipulated video clip.
Commentators jump on these bandwagons without a second thought for context, nuance, or basic human empathy.
Facts do not matter to the mob. Once the narrative is set -- that women have become too "modern," too "independent," and too "uncontrolled" -- the digital machinery of character assassination goes into overdrive.
From faceless bots to female envy
What makes this digital ecosystem particularly toxic is its composition.
It is propelled not just by men hiding behind pseudonyms, but also by a distinct psychological undercurrent of internalized misogyny.
On one hand, we have the legions of nameless male profiles -- the virtual moral police whose own lives are often defined by frustration, stagnation, and a deep-seated insecurity regarding modern, autonomous women.
Their online vitriol is an outlet for impotent rage against a changing world where women refuse to remain silent, subservient second-class citizens.
Protected by the anonymity of a screen, these men project their anxieties onto viral targets, seeking a toxic sense of community and validation from other like-minded misogynists.
On the other hand, we must confront an uncomfortable truth: This phenomenon is not exclusively male.
Often, women themselves participate in the shaming, driven by a potent mix of social conditioning and deep-seated envy. In societies where female worth has historically been tied to strict conformity, seeing another woman break the mold can trigger a defensive reaction.
Some women, having internalized patriarchal standards to survive, view independent or non-conformist women as a threat to the fragile security they have carved out for themselves.
By joining the mob, they signal their own "purity" and conformity. This betrayal from within is perhaps the most tragic aspect of the cycle, as it fractures solidarity precisely when it is needed most.
Call for social ostracization
We have reached a critical juncture in the digital evolution of South Asia. The line between online commentary and real-world harm has long since blurred.
When internet trolls normalize victim-blaming, they create a cultural climate where violence against women is minimized, excused, or implicitly encouraged.
This behaviour cannot simply be brushed aside as "just internet noise" or the ramblings of "trolls being trolls."
These voices shape public perception, intimidate survivors into silence, and deter women from seeking justice or participating fully in public life.
Combating this requires a fundamental cultural reset.
We must strip away the digital armour that emboldens these cowards.
Anonymity on social media should no longer be a free pass to terrorize victims of crime or ruin reputations with impunity.
Platforms must be held accountable for enabling networks of abuse and algorithmic amplification of misogyny.
More importantly, the remedy must come from society itself.
These shamelessly insensitive remarks and baseless accusations must be actively confronted and socially shunned.
Just as we would condemn someone for making excuses for a thief or a murderer in a physical room, we must call out those who excuse abuse and degradation in the digital room.
Friends, family members, colleagues, and community leaders must make it clear that victim-blaming and casual misogyny are not "opinions" to be debated -- they are moral failures.
Until the cost of participating in online harassment becomes too high -- until social circles, workplaces, and public platforms make it socially untenable to bully and blame women -- the digital public square will remain a dangerous frontier.
It is time to drag these faceless inquisitors out of the shadows and hold them to the light of accountability.
Women in our society deserve nothing less than a culture that protects their dignity, respects their autonomy, and refuses to negotiate with the malice of the mob.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

Ackerman hits century as South Africa bounce back
item.description:
CRICKET-RSA-BAN-TEST

Marques Ackerman hit an aggressive century as South Africa bounced back on the second day of the first Test against Bangladesh at the Wanderers Stadium on Monday.

The left-handed Ackerman struck 157 off 164 balls as South Africa made 287 for four in reply to Bangladesh's first innings of 400.

Ackerman, in his third Test, and the recalled Zubayr Hamza, who made 83, put on 202 for the second wicket. They came together after the experienced Aiden Markram was caught behind off Hasan Mahmud for four in the second over of South Africa's innings.

Earlier, Bangladesh made their highest total against South Africa.

Litton Das, resuming on 92, scored 120 as the tourists added 73 runs to their overnight total of 327 for six for the loss of their remaining four wickets.

Ackerman and Hamza had to survive some hostile new ball bowling by Mahmud and Taskin Ahmed but took control on a true batting surface as the ball lost its shine.

Hamza, playing in his eighth Test but his first in more than two years, put in a strong claim to establish himself in South Africa's problematic number three batting position. He is the eighth player to be tried at three since Shukri Conrad became coach in 2023.

Hamza hit 12 boundaries in a 129-ball innings before he was caught behind in the first over bowled by part-time left-arm spinner Mominul Haque.

Ackerman, who made 95 in his second Test appearance against Australia last month, again displayed a fearless approach, using his feet and playing a variety of wristy strokes.

He showed no nerves as he cruised through the nineties, reaching his century off 125 balls. He then went on an all-out assault, scoring 57 more runs off 39 deliveries before he was caught in the deep off Mahmud. Ackerman hit 21 fours and a six.

Ackerman's dismissal brought Bangladesh back into the contest and Mahmud claimed his third wicket when Matthew Breetzke was caught behind for two.

Mahmud could have had a fourth scalp but Ryan Rickelton survived a difficult chance to wicketkeeper Das off the first ball he faced.

item.title: Minimum wage board meeting delay raises concern
item.description:
The third meeting of the Minimum Wage Board, where garment factory owners were scheduled to submit their proposals for the new minimum wage structure for readymade garment (RMG) workers, was abruptly postponed on Monday morning (November 16).
Despite owners having completed their preparations in advance to submit the proposal, Board Secretary Raisa Afroz issued an official notice Monday morning announcing that the 11:00 AM meeting at the Department of Labour had been postponed due to "unavoidable circumstances" upon instructions from the authorities.
Speaking to reporters regarding the sudden suspension, Minimum Wage Board chairman Syed Azad Subhani stated: "One of our permanent board members suddenly fell ill and had to be admitted to the hospital. It would not be appropriate to hold the board meeting without him. That is why we have postponed it. The new date for the next meeting will be announced shortly."
Following the postponement, the apex trade bodies of the apparel sector—the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA)—issued a joint press release signed by BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan and BKMEA President Mohammad Hatem.
The two organizations stated that the owners' side was fully prepared to present its wage proposal at Monday's meeting.
Pointing out that the new wage structure is scheduled to come into effect on December 1, they noted that timely completion of the board's activities would allow factories the necessary time to prepare for paying increased wages.
Accordingly, the trade bodies urged the authorities to announce a new date for the postponed meeting as soon as possible.
Meanwhile, Taslima Akhter, president of the Bangladesh Garment Sramik Samhati, told Dhaka Tribune: "We have heard that the meeting was postponed because a board member fell ill. We want the owners' proposal to be accepted within the stipulated timeframe so that wage-fixing discussions can move forward. To finalize and implement the new pay structure, the board must convene quickly.”
Garment workers have been protesting since last month demanding a wage hike. In response, the government formed a new Minimum Wage Board on November 1.
At the board's first meeting on November 4, it was announced that the new wage structure would take effect from December 1.
During the second meeting on November 9, workers' representative Babul Akhter proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk32,000.
As the owners' side was unable to present its proposal on that day, they were granted four working days, which led up to Monday's scheduled session.
Previously, the last minimum wage for garment workers was announced in November 2023, raising the minimum monthly pay from Tk8,000 to Tk12,500.

item.title: How late HIV detection claimed a 27-year-old in Bangladesh
item.description:
His mother clung to her son’s body as it lay on a stretcher in the intensive care unit of Dhaka’s Infectious Diseases Hospital in Mohakhali, crying inconsolably, as though letting go of him would mean accepting that he was never coming home.
He was just 27.
A former student of two of Bangladesh’s most respected educational institutions, Tayeeb (pseudonym) had completed his master’s degree about two years earlier and was looking for a job, with the prospect of a professional life still ahead of him.
His family was financially comfortable, and he had the support and opportunities that many young people could only hope for.
Yet none of these could protect him from an infection that, until he became critically ill, his family did not even know he had.
Tayeeb died on Monday after being diagnosed with HIV and cryptococcal meningitis, a potentially life-threatening fungal infection that affects the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord, according to doctors at the hospital.
For his family, the diagnosis was devastating.
They had never known he was living with HIV, and by the time the infection was discovered, his condition had already deteriorated severely.
According to his uncle, Tayeeb initially sought treatment at a private hospital after developing a persistent headache.
Medical examinations revealed a fungal infection in his brain and an HIV infection, following which he was referred to the Infectious Diseases Hospital.
His uncle said the family learned of the HIV diagnosis on October 15.
They had no clear idea how he had contracted the virus; although the family reported no known history of blood transfusion, they could not identify a likely route of transmission.
Doctors told the family that the infection had reached an advanced stage, his uncle said.
Tayeeb’s story challenges the assumption that HIV is a problem confined to people living in poverty or without access to education and resources.
He came from a financially comfortable family and had studied at some of the country’s leading institutions, yet the infection remained undetected until serious complications had developed.
At the Infectious Diseases Hospital, his final days unfolded amid a heavy burden of HIV patients.
Superintendent Dr FA Asma Khan told this correspondent that 24 people living with HIV were admitted to the hospital on the same day, against its capacity of 25 beds for such patients.
More than 2,000 people were enrolled on the hospital’s HIV services to receive medication, she said.
“Today, we have 19 measles patients and 24 HIV patients,” Khan said.
The hospital figures offer a snapshot of the pressure on one of Bangladesh’s key public facilities for infectious diseases, as the country records a sharp rise in newly detected HIV infections.
The National HIV/AIDS Situation Report 2025 recorded 1,891 new HIV cases between November 2024 and October 2025, up from 1,438 in the preceding 12-month period, an increase of about 31.5%.
It also recorded 254 HIV/AIDS-related deaths during the period, compared with 326 a year earlier.
An estimated 17,480 people were living with HIV in Bangladesh in 2025.
But the challenge extends beyond diagnosis and access to medication.
For many people living with HIV, stigma and discrimination remain formidable obstacles to seeking treatment and living a normal life.
A health worker involved in a Global Fund-supported project to control HIV in Bangladesh said many of the patients encountered by their team were men, including men who have sex with men (MSM) and bisexual men.
Many were also strikingly young, often just 22 or 23 years old, including university students, the worker said.
At an age when they should be pursuing their studies, building careers and making plans for the future, these young men are instead having to navigate an HIV diagnosis alongside the fear of rejection and social discrimination.
The worker stressed that people who take antiretroviral medication regularly can live healthy, normal lives.
The greater obstacles, in many cases, are a lack of awareness, fear and the social taboos surrounding the virus.
The worker also described instances in which doctors had allegedly refused to perform surgery on people living with HIV out of fear that other patients might become infected, a misconception that can deny patients essential medical care.
An infectious disease specialist who works closely with people living with HIV said such fears were medically unfounded, explaining that HIV does not spread through ordinary contact between patients and that standard infection-control measures and proper sterilisation procedures are sufficient to prevent transmission in healthcare settings.
A person's HIV status alone is not a reason to deny them surgery.
Doctors say HIV can remain undetected for years, allowing the virus to progressively weaken the immune system without the person knowing they are infected.
By the time symptoms become severe, patients may already be vulnerable to infections, illnesses that a healthy immune system would ordinarily be able to fight off.
Cryptococcal meningitis is one such infection, and earlier HIV diagnosis can allow appropriate care to begin before such life-threatening complications develop.
For Tayeeb’s family, however, the questions remain unanswered: when he contracted the virus, how long he had been living with it, and whether he had any indication of his condition before he became seriously ill.
His uncle said the family has been searching for an answer ever since.
“We asked his friends. The counsellors asked him, and the doctor asked him separately. He could not tell us how it happened, and he could not even imagine it,” the uncle said.
“We went through the reasons one by one, three or four of them. The first was sexual transmission. But no, he is a man of prayer. He reads the Quran. He does not even smoke. Then we thought maybe it was drugs or injections. But his friends come to our house, and they call me mama. They told us that when he had to get an injection, he would take one of them along with him, because he was so afraid of needles. How could he take drugs?”
“Then we asked about blood. But he never needed a transfusion. Whether he gave blood to someone while he was at university, I do not know,”
“It is simply a misfortune,” the uncle said.
He had studied, graduated and was looking for a beginning.
However, he never got the chance because of HIV.
His death is a reminder that timely testing can be critical to preventing a manageable infection from progressing into a life-threatening illness.

item.title: Dengue death toll crosses 500 as three die in 24hrs
item.description:
Three more people died from dengue and 1,598 were hospitalized with the mosquito-borne disease in the 24 hours till 8am Monday, taking the country's death toll to 502 this year.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), a total of 164,107 dengue patients have been hospitalized across the country so far this year.
Of the newly hospitalized patients, 673 were in Dhaka Division, 61 in Mymensingh Division, 251 in Chattogram Division, 201 in Khulna Division, 145 in Rajshahi Division, 71 in Rangpur Division, 185 in Barisal Division and 11 in Sylhet Division.

Last year, a total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, while 413 died from the mosquito-borne disease.

item.title: Bangladesh’s childcare crisis is holding women back from work
item.description:
Four in every 10 mothers in urban Bangladesh who are not employed say childcare responsibilities are a major reason they cannot enter the workforce, exposing how the lack of affordable and accessible daycare is limiting women’s economic participation.
According to a policy brief titled “Childcare in Bangladesh: What Families Need, What Providers Deliver, and Where the Gaps Remain,” published by the World Bank’s South Asia Gender Innovation Lab, 38.4% of non-working mothers in urban areas identified childcare responsibilities as a key barrier to taking up employment.
The findings point to a significant gap between Bangladesh’s ambition to increase women’s participation in the economy and the everyday challenges faced by mothers who cannot find reliable care for their children.
The problem is particularly concerning amid a large population of young people who are neither in education, employment nor training (NEET). Around 9.6 million people aged 15-29 fall into this category in Bangladesh, with women accounting for approximately two-thirds of the total.
The World Bank’s research draws on demand-side surveys involving 1,700 respondents in rural and semi-urban areas and nearly 3,000 mothers in urban industrial areas. It also maps 514 childcare providers in Dhaka and examines the operations of 335 of them.
The scale of the challenge is particularly evident in Dhaka, where more than 21 million people have access to only 514 identified childcare providers, including government, private, non-profit, madrasa-based and home-based facilities.
The average capacity of the surveyed centers was just 55 children, indicating a substantial mismatch between the availability of childcare services and the needs of families in the capital.
The study found that 57% of government childcare centers had waiting lists, limiting access to some of the most affordable formal services.
Only 0.1% of mothers in urban areas reported using institutional daycare facilities, while around 20% relied on home-based childcare providers.
The findings also highlight the financial barriers facing families. Around 61% of urban mothers reported having no formal or family-based support for childcare. Among these mothers, 87% said they could not afford paid childcare services.
Private commercial daycare centers are largely concentrated in higher-income neighborhoods, while low- and lower-middle-income families have fewer affordable options.
The study suggests that the availability of childcare alone is not enough. Parents also consider distance, affordability and trust when deciding where to leave their children.
Mothers in semi-urban areas were willing to pay an additional Tk1,000-1,700 per month for childcare facilities closer to their homes rather than near their workplaces or training centers.
They were also willing to pay up to Tk1,200 more per month to leave their children with a familiar and trusted caregiver rather than an unfamiliar professional provider.
These preferences indicate that families often priorities convenient locations and trusted caregivers over conventional institutional arrangements.
The World Bank’s assessment notes that families want childcare services that are affordable, close to home, trustworthy and supportive of children’s development. However, existing formal services remain limited, unevenly distributed and beyond the financial reach of many low-income households.
Bangladesh enacted the Child Daycare Centre Act in 2021, providing for registration, inspections and penalties for violations. However, significant gaps remain in translating the legal framework into accessible and quality childcare services.
The World Bank’s Women, Business and the Law 2026 report gives Bangladesh a score of zero out of 100 on the relevant supportive-framework indicators, highlighting the lack of the necessary institutional arrangements and policy support to make childcare provisions effective in practice.
The study also identifies substantial differences in service quality between formal and informal providers.
Government-run centers generally perform better in terms of trained staff, physical safety and food arrangements. However, their limited availability and waiting lists restrict access.
By contrast, none of the surveyed home-based childcare providers had received formal training, while many lacked basic safety equipment.
The World Bank’s Early Learning Partnership framework identifies seven essential elements of quality childcare: trained caregivers, warm and responsive interactions, safe and healthy environments, appropriate caregiver-to-child ratios, structured daily routines, play-based learning and regular engagement with parents.
Beyond the shortage of childcare facilities, social attitudes and household decision-making also influence women’s ability to work.
Surveys in rural and semi-urban areas found that majorities of both men and women supported women’s participation in economic activities. However, opposition within families, particularly from male members, remained a significant obstacle.
Around 90% of wives surveyed supported women’s income-earning activities, compared with approximately 67% of husbands.
The findings suggest that expanding childcare facilities must go hand in hand with efforts to change social attitudes and encourage men to share responsibility for childcare and household work.
The World Bank research highlights the importance of social and behavioral change (SBC) initiatives targeting men and families to strengthen support for women’s economic participation.
The World Bank argues that expanding large institutional daycare centers through public funding alone may not be sufficient to address the country’s childcare gap.
Instead, it recommends recognizing and improving home-based childcare services, particularly in densely populated and low-income communities.
One initiative is the Recovery and Advancement of Informal Sector Employment (RAISE) project, jointly supported by the World Bank and the Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF). Under the initiative, women in densely populated areas receive training and financial support to establish childcare micro-enterprises.
The study also calls for a more flexible regulatory approach. Excessively punitive requirements and bureaucratic procedures could force small informal providers to close, further reducing childcare options for low-income families.
Instead, inspections should be accompanied by training, first-aid kits, childproofing materials and practical guidance to improve safety and service quality.
Other priorities include targeted subsidies to make childcare affordable for low-income households and revisions to the 2021 law to provide appropriate legal recognition and protection for different childcare models, including public, private and home-based services.
The findings underline that childcare is not simply a family or social welfare issue. It is also an economic concern that directly affects women’s ability to earn, build careers and contribute to national growth.
Without affordable, accessible and reliable childcare, a significant proportion of Bangladesh’s potential female workforce may continue to remain outside the labor market.

item.title: Information Commission resumes RTI complaint hearings after nearly two years
item.description:
The Information Commission Bangladesh has resumed hearing complaints filed under the Right to Information (RTI) Act after nearly two years.
The Commission held hearings on five complaints on Monday, disposing of three of them and fixing dates for further hearings on the remaining two.
Chief Information Commissioner Prof Dr Nahreen Islam Khan, along with Information Commissioners S A M Mahfuzur Rahman and Khan Mohammad Abul Hossain, conducted the hearings.
With the Commission remaining non-functional for an extended period, a total of 917 complaints were filed over the past two years. The government reconstituted the Information Commission on October 17.
After assuming office, the newly constituted Commission adopted a 100-day action plan, prioritizing the disposal of pending complaints. As part of the initiative, it is working to expedite the hearing and resolution process.
The complaints heard on Monday concerned the non-disclosure of information relating to recruitment by various public and private institutions, land ownership and income-expenditure accounts of institutions, development projects and allocations of local government bodies, reasons for cancellation of appointment letters, recruitment examination answer scripts, and the leasing of government property.

item.title: EC to hold first-phase UP elections in 1,026 unions on Jan 21
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) will hold elections to 1,026 Union Parishads (UPs) under 131 upazilas in the first phase on January 21.
The decision was taken at an EC meeting held at the Nirbachan Bhaban in the city's Agargaon area on Monday.
After the meeting, Election Commissioner Abul Fazal Md Sanaullah briefed journalists on the decisions.
The EC has planned to arrange elections to more than 4000 UPs in the five-phase election in the early next year.
The lists of UPs for each phase election will be published on the EC website by next Thursday, said the Election Commissioner.
According to the plan, elections in the second phase will be held in 1,113 UPs under 129 upazilas, the third phase in 1,002 UPs under 118 upazilas, the fourth phase in 793 UPs under 93 upazilas and the fifth phase in 356 UPs under 37 upazilas.
The Election Commission has also planned to hold discussions with political parties ahead of the UP elections and complete the dialogue by December 10.
Abul Fazl said the matter was discussed at Monday's meeting and the commission plans to invite registered political parties for discussions over three days, either late this month or early December, following their registration serial numbers.
Asked whether any political party had demanded the deployment of army personnel in local government elections, he said the commission had not received any such demand so far.
The commission would take necessary measures after assessing whether the agencies concerned could effectively perform their duties in particular areas and maintain the election environment, he added.
The meeting also discussed ongoing problems with National Identity Card (NID) services and smart card printing.
Abul Fazl said the software used for smart card printing had been experiencing problems over the last four to five days. However, he claimed that no NID services had been suspended due to the problem and said efforts were underway to resolve it.
The commission also decided that Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) would no longer be used in any election.
The meeting reviewed progress made by a committee formed to determine how the EVMs currently in storage would be disposed of.
Abul Fazl said the commission had received an update on the committee's progress.
Asked about environmental concerns and financial losses associated with destroying the EVMs, he said these issues had not yet been discussed by the commission.

item.title: ‘Taste of America’ in Dhaka: Ambassador pushes for wider US food access
item.description:
The US embassy in Dhaka organized a day-long food and agricultural products exhibition, “Taste of America”, at the Sheraton Hotel in Banani on Monday to mark 250 years of US independence and promote agricultural trade between Bangladesh and the United States.
Speaking as the chief guest at the opening session, US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent T Christensen said reducing trade barriers would allow consumers in Bangladesh to access a wider variety of products at lower prices.
The exhibition showcased agricultural products, food items and culinary ingredients, including premium US beef. It aimed to highlight the quality and commercial potential of American food products to Bangladeshi importers, chefs, restaurants and businesses in the hospitality sector.
The ambassador said facilitating the entry of more US products into Bangladesh was one of his key priorities. Expanding trade would give American companies access to new markets while enabling Bangladeshi businesses to import high-quality products and ingredients, benefiting both economies.
He said import costs would decrease once the trade agreement between the 2 countries came into effect, as reduced tariffs would make American food imports easier and more affordable.
On food safety, he said products must pass prescribed tests before they can be exported to the US market. He added that the trade agreement emphasized high standards of food safety, intellectual property protection and an effective regulatory system.
Highlighting the market situation in Bangladesh, Christensen said import restrictions and an unregulated market system drove up the prices of many products. Counterfeit and adulterated food products also forced consumers to spend more while creating uncertainty about quality.
“Every family has the right to safe and quality food at fair prices,” he said, adding that initiatives to gradually reduce trade barriers would continue.
The ambassador said American beef, known internationally for steaks, also had commercial potential alongside traditional Bangladeshi dishes such as biryani, polao, mezban and tehari.
He said grain-based feeding produced distinctive marbling, tenderness and flavor, while the US Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Choice and Prime grades were internationally recognized as high-quality products.
He said there was currently no opportunity to legally purchase American beef in Bangladesh, meaning those seeking premium American steak had to travel to Bangkok, Singapore, Tokyo or the United States.
Photo: Courtesy
The US embassy would work with the Bangladesh government to ensure commercial access to premium US beef in the country, he added.
Christensen also said that following the approval of tariff concessions in 2025, Bangladesh had become the ninth-largest buyer of US wheat. He called on the country to import more wheat, process it locally and use it in restaurants and cafes.
Halal-slaughtered beef imported from Iowa, the ambassador's home state, was served to guests at the event.
The exhibition also featured a cupcake-making competition in which Bangladeshi bakers used American ingredients. Business networking sessions brought together importers, chefs, restaurants and hospitality businesses, while live music performances were also held.

item.title: PM urges students to help keep Dhaka clean, protect environment
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday emphasized the role of students in keeping Dhaka clean and protecting the environment, encouraging them to plant more trees, care for animals and wildlife, and develop skills and a sense of social responsibility to become worthy citizens of the country.
“Give trees as gifts to your loved ones on their birthdays. Planting more trees will improve the environment. You may think, ‘what do I gain if the environment improves?’ We all will benefit,” he said.
The prime minister made the remarks when he met students, who had come to visit the National Parliament and watch its proceedings, during the Maghrib prayer break in the evening.
Tarique also stressed the importance of sports and caring for animals and other living creatures, saying human beings were the best of creation and had a responsibility to protect nature and wildlife.
He said students should develop skills and a sense of social responsibility to prepare themselves to become capable citizens who could contribute to the country and society.
The Prime Minister also underlined the need for vocational education, sports and language learning alongside academic studies.
Addressing the students, he said the government was introducing vocational education in schools and colleges, which would be compulsory from Class IX.
“Everyone must be properly prepared for the future. We are introducing vocational education in schools and colleges. Students will have to take vocational education compulsorily from Class IX,” Tarique said.
He also said students should take part in the Notun Kuri Sports program, which would offer six to seven different sports disciplines, allowing them to choose according to their interests.
He said sports should receive equal importance alongside academic studies.
The Prime Minister also spoke about plans to develop students' proficiency in multiple languages, saying everyone should learn an additional language apart from their mother tongue.
Students would be able to choose their preferred language from six to seven options, including English, Mandarin and Japanese, he said.
Earlier, 43 students who secured GPA-5 in the SSC examinations and six teachers from five educational institutions in Dohar upazila in Dhaka, 15 Class XII students and four teachers from the capital's Monipur High School, and nine students from Chandpur Medical College visited the National Parliament and observed parliamentary proceedings.
As part of the visit, they attended a briefing, visited the parliament library and took photographs at the North Plaza of the National Parliament.

item.title: Garment factories in Savar, Ashulia return to normal operations
item.description:
Garment factories in Savar and Ashulia have maintained normal production following several days of tension, with most workers returning to work peacefully on Monday morning.
A visit to different industrial areas in the morning found workers entering factories within their scheduled hours.
However, law enforcement agencies remained on alert to prevent any untoward incidents. Additional police and members of other forces were deployed at key points and in front of factories.
Despite the overall improvement, production remained suspended at several factories in Ashulia.
Industrial police said more than 30 factories across the industrial zone remained closed due to labour unrest, while workers at two factories were observing work stoppages. All other factories remained open.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police of Industrial Police-1, said the situation in Savar, Ashulia and Dhamrai under his jurisdiction was normal, with operations running smoothly.
"Factory owners have kept around 30 factories closed for various reasons. Operations have been normal everywhere since morning. Workers at only two factories are observing work stoppages. No disorder has been reported elsewhere," he said.
He said the industrial zone has around 800 garment factories, of which approximately 30 remain closed.
Of these, 27 factories have been closed under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, four are observing general holidays, and nine have been declared closed indefinitely. Workers at two factories joined work but later stopped working, he added.
He said factory owners and other stakeholders all want stability in the garment sector.
Khairul Mamun Mintu, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Sweater Workers Trade Union Centre, said the situation had remained normal since morning.
"Some factories that were previously closed have reopened. Workers have joined work, and the situation remains normal so far. In a small number of factories where workers had joined but were not working, holidays have been declared under Section 13(1) of the Labour Act, following the 'no work, no pay' principle. Apart from these, the situation across the industrial zone is normal," he said.

item.title: Pallabi child rape-murder: Swapna helped Sohel out of fear, prosecution tells HC
item.description:
The wife of Sohel Rana, who was sentenced to death for the rape and murder of an eight-year-old child Pallabi, was so afraid of her husband that she helped him in the killing, the prosecution told the High Court on Monday.
The submission came during the hearing on the death references and appeals filed by Sohel and his wife, Swapna Akter, before a High Court bench led by Justice Bhishmadev Chakrabortty.
The prosecution concluded its arguments on the day. Deputy Attorney General Barrister Mohammad Osman Chowdhury represented the state.
According to the case documents, the child's father lived with his family in a rented flat in Pallabi. He worked at a private office in Banani.
Sohel Rana and Swapna Akter lived in another flat in the same building. The child was a second-grade student at a local school.
On May 19, the child was raped and murdered. Sohel later escaped by cutting through the window grille of the room.
Police took Swapna into custody after receiving information through the national emergency helpline 999. Sohel was later arrested in front of Fatullah police station in Narayanganj.
The child's father filed a case with Pallabi police station over the incident. On May 21, Sohel gave a confessional statement before a court under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Both accused were subsequently sent to jail.
On May 25, the investigating officer, Sub-Inspector Ahiduzzaman of Pallabi police station, submitted a charge sheet against Sohel and Swapna. The case was sent to the tribunal for trial on the same day.
The trial began on June 1 with the framing of charges against the two accused. The following day, the prosecution presented 16 witnesses, completing the recording of testimony in a single day.
The accused were examined under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, on June 3.
On June 7, Judge Masrur Salequin of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children's Violence Suppression Tribunal sentenced both accused to death.
The tribunal also fined Sohel Tk5 lakh and Swapna Tk2 lakh, directing that the money be paid to the child's legal heirs.
The verdict was delivered just 19 days after the murder.
The death references containing the case records were subsequently sent to the High Court for confirmation of the sentences. Both convicts later filed jail appeals before the High Court.

item.title: Prime Bank signs MoU with BEPZA Public School and College
item.description:
Prime Bank PLC has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Bepza Public School and College under its flagship PrimeAcademia initiative, aimed at providing tailored banking solutions and enhancing financial convenience for the institution, its teachers, students and parents.
Through this partnership, Prime Bank will extend its comprehensive range of PrimeAcademia banking solutions to the institution and its eligible stakeholders.
The initiative is designed to facilitate digital fee collection, institutional banking, payroll management, savings facilities for teachers and students, and other financial services tailored to the needs of the academic community.
The signing ceremony was attended by Shaila Abedin, SEVP and head of liability & women banking; Sarker Mehadhi Reza, SVP & regional head, Chittagong region; and Ruma Ghosh, branch manager, Karnafuli EPZ branch, representing Prime Bank.
Representing Bepza Public School and College were Major Md Anwarul Kabir (retd), principal, and Mohammad Nuruzzaman, director (accounts), Bepza KEPZ Zone .
Prime Bank continues to strengthen its engagement with educational institutions across Bangladesh, offering integrated financial solutions that support institutional efficiency and promote a culture of savings and financial awareness among the next generation.

item.title: SahajMobile secures up to $25m for smartphone financing
item.description:
SahajMobile has closed a credit facility with ALMA, enabling total borrowings of up to $25 million through its US holding company, HR Consortium USA, Inc.
Part of its broader Series A financing led by Beacon Peak Partners, the facility will support smartphone financing for underserved customers across Bangladesh.
Since launching in 2024, SahajMobile has helped tens of thousands of customers access smartphones through installment financing via more than 3,300 retail partners.
Combining proprietary technology, international credit expertise and local operations, it aims to finance one million customers by 2027, expanding connectivity and financial inclusion, particularly for women and rural communities.
Bangladesh’s credit and connectivity gaps remain substantial.
In 2024, approximately 16 million adults borrowed from formal sources, while roughly 76 million—62% of adults—did not own a personal smartphone.
Smartphone shipments reached 10.6 million units in 2025, up 22% year on year, underscoring demand for devices that connect people to the digital economy.
“There is an enormous credit story in this region that deserves more attention from institutional investors,” said Rafsun Faiz, founder and CEO of SahajMobile.
“We see an underserved market with real demand for credit. This financing will help us continue our growth and connect global capital with everyday borrowers across Bangladesh, starting with smartphone financing.”
SahajMobile’s management team brings lending, credit and technology experience from Guggenheim Partners, BAWAG, Google, Qualia, Macquarie, BlackRock and Kiavi, alongside local entrepreneurship and operating experience through co-founder and managing director Abu Al Motalib.
The team applies institutional underwriting, structuring and portfolio management to a market whose customers and operating conditions it knows firsthand.
Its proprietary technology supports financing across multiple smartphone brands and retail channels.
By combining capital, credit assessment and local distribution, SahajMobile makes installment financing accessible while maintaining responsible lending practices.
SahajMobile BD Ltd. has also received a No Objection Certificate from Bangladesh Bank.
The pilot prioritizes low-income people without smartphones and underserved areas approved by Bangladesh Bank, subject to operating conditions and ongoing monitoring.
“Digitizing Bangladesh starts with getting people connected,” said Abu Al Motalib, co-founder and managing director of SahajMobile.
“For someone in a rural community, a smartphone can be a tool to find work, reach customers, receive payments and access essential services. We want to make financing available for an asset that can help people earn, including women, who remain extremely underserved in the market.”

item.title: Adcelerate brings AI-powered ad campaign for Honor 600S 5G
item.description:
What if an advertisement could do more than show people what technology can do? What if they could experience it themselves?
Adcelerete Technologies Limited has introduced an interactive digital advertising campaign for the Honor 600S 5G, bringing an AI-powered image-to-video experience directly to audiences through the web.
The campaign features two advertising formats: an interactive floating experience and an image overlay placement within a digital news portal environment.
Both formats bring the Honor campaign into everyday digital browsing, offering audiences an opportunity to explore its creative concept through direct interaction.
At the centre of the floating experience is a browser-based image-to-video interface. Users can upload an image from their gallery or camera, enter a creative prompt and choose between portrait (9:16) and landscape (16:9) video formats.
The interface also includes an optional start-frame input. Users can generate a five-second video, preview the result and download their creation.
The image overlay format complements this experience by presenting the Honor creative within a news-style web portal environment, introducing the campaign alongside the content audiences are already browsing.
The campaign draws on the creative proposition of the Honor 600S 5G, which features AI Image to Video 2.0.
The feature is designed to help users turn images into video content through generative AI.
Its availability and service terms are subject to regional conditions and software updates.
Through this campaign, Adcelerete combines interactive media placements with an AI-led creative experience, giving the brand a way to demonstrate its product proposition beyond conventional display advertising.
It also reflects the growing opportunity for brands to use interactive formats to make technology-led campaigns more tangible and engaging.
The campaign marks another step in Adcelerete’s exploration of advertising formats that connect brand communication with audience experience.

item.title: Midland Bank holds 201st executive committee meeting
item.description:
The 201st executive committee meeting of the board of directors Midland Bank PLC was held on Sunday, November 15 at the board room of the bank's head office at Gulshan, Dhaka.
The meeting was presided over by Rezaul Karim, chairman of the executive committee.
Ahsan Khan Chowdhury, Master Abul Kashem, Mostafizur Rahman, Mohammed Helal Miah, Riaz Ahmed Choudhury, and other members of the committee were also present.
Other attendees included Imtiaz U Ahmed, managing director of Midland Bank PLC; Md Zahid Hossain, deputy managing director & chief risk officer; and Md Nazmul Huda Sarkar, deputy managing director & chief technology officer.
The executive committee engaged in discussions concerning various, business, strategic and operational issues.
Key areas of focus included enhancing the bank's overall performance, upholding good governance, and fostering sustainable business growth.
This 201st meeting represents a significant milestone in the bank's ongoing commitment to achieving its strategic objectives and maintaining operational excellence.

item.title: Pubali Bank Wins ICSB National Award for corporate governance excellence
item.description:
Pubali Bank PLC has received the bronze award in the general banking category at the 13th ICSB National Award for Corporate Governance Excellence, organized by the Institute of Chartered Secretaries of Bangladesh (ICSB).
Minister of Commerce, Textiles and Jute, and Industries Khandakar Abdul Muktadir handed over the award to the bank’s deputy managing director Mohammad Shahadat Hossain and company secretary Md Anisur Rahman, at the award ceremony held at Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel, Dhaka recently.
Mohammad Liton Miah, chief financial officer, Muhammad Mahmudur Rahman, assistant general manager, and Md Ashraf-UZ-Zaman, assistant general manager of Pubali Bank PLC, were also present on that award ceremony.
The ceremony was attended by several distinguished guests, including Hafiz Ahmed Chowdhury, secretary, Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Sharif Uddin Ahmed Choudhury, secretary, Ministry of Commerce; Masud Khan, chairman of the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC); and Mohammad Shahjahan, president of ICSB.

item.title: BCIC chairman warns of strict action against fertilizer irregularities
item.description:
Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC) Chairman Md Babul Mia has warned of strict action against anyone involved in irregularities or corruption in fertilizer distribution and storage in the northern region.
He has also assured farmers that the country has adequate fertilizer stocks and there is no actual shortage.
Babul Mia made the remarks at a meeting of the monitoring committee on fertilizer transportation, storage and stock management at Rangpur Circuit House on November 13, said a press release.
The meeting, organised by the Rangpur district administration, was chaired by Rangpur Deputy Commissioner Israt Jahan. It focused on the progress of the project to construct 34 buffer warehouses and the current fertilizer stock, transportation and storage situation in the region.
Earlier, on November 12 and 13, the BCIC chairman visited under-construction buffer warehouses in Thakurgaon, Panchagarh, Lalmonirhat and Rangpur to assess the project's progress and the overall fertilizer supply situation.
During the visits, he inspected construction work and reviewed fertilizer transportation, storage and stock management at the sites.
He instructed the contractors and officials concerned to maintain construction quality and complete the work within the stipulated timeframe.
He also stressed the need to maintain adequate stocks in line with farmers' demand and ensure close monitoring of transportation and distribution to keep fertilizer supplies uninterrupted.
Addressing the meeting, Babul Mia said the government was taking all necessary measures to strengthen fertilizer supply and storage facilities in the northern region.
He warned that anyone involved in fertilizer-related irregularities or corruption would be brought to justice.
He said misleading claims about an artificial fertilizer shortage, spread by unscrupulous quarters, were creating confusion among farmers.
To prevent rumours and ensure transparency, he urged district administrations and officials concerned to regularly monitor fertilizer stocks and distribution.
He also advised farmers not to panic or stockpile more fertilizer than they need.

item.title: BADC project targets higher pulse, oilseed production
item.description:
The Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) is implementing a project to boost domestic production of pulses and oilseeds, reduce import dependence and strengthen the country's food and nutritional security.
According to a press release, the country's annual demand for pulses is 2.5 million tonnes, while domestic production stands at only 937,000 tonnes. Similarly, annual demand for edible oil is 2.482 million tonnes, against domestic production of 1.064 million tonnes, according to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE).
The shortfall forces Bangladesh to import substantial quantities of pulses and edible oil, putting pressure on foreign currency reserves.
Approved by the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (Ecnec) on December 8, 2024, the project, titled "Strengthening Sustainable Nutritional Security through the Production of Pulses and Oilseeds (Phase 2)," will run from July 2025 to June 2029.
The project aims to produce 18,000 tonnes of quality seeds and distribute them among farmers. Its activities cover 42 districts, two city corporations and 200 upazilas across eight divisions through three farms, three seed processing centres and 12 contract-farming zones.
Project estimates suggest that the targeted seed production will generate an additional 256,499 tonnes of agricultural produce worth Tk2,964 crore over the project's duration.
During the 2025-26 fiscal year, the project produced 3,723.112 tonnes of pulse and oilseed seeds through contract farming. These included lentil, mung bean, mustard, soybean, groundnut and sunflower seeds, which are being distributed for the 2026-27 cropping season.
Their use is expected to generate an additional 51,455 tonnes of crops worth Tk597.57 crore across approximately 606,360 acres.
The project, costing Tk265.78 crore, also includes training for 2,000 contract farmers in seed production, processing and storage.
Project Director Dr Md Shafiqul Islam is overseeing implementation, including field-level activities and seed production and distribution.
The initiative is expected to increase farmers' incomes, create rural employment and reduce the country's reliance on imported pulses and edible oil.

item.title: Satkhira municipality fails to ensure safe water for households
item.description:
Residents of Satkhira municipality have complained that the water supplied by the local authorities is often contaminated with dirt, foul-smelling substances, and even worms, making it unfit for drinking and household use.
Many families are consequently forced to spend Tk1,500-2,000 a month buying drinking water. Against this backdrop, civil society representatives have proposed eight recommendations to address the crisis, particularly in low-income communities.
The proposals include making water supply services affordable, promoting rooftop rainwater harvesting and household wells, developing rainwater reservoirs, and installing public water taps in slums and densely populated areas.
They also called for protecting ponds and other water bodies from encroachment, regularly testing municipal and jarred water for arsenic, iron, salinity and pH levels, and publishing the results online.
The recommendations were presented at a citizens' dialogue titled “Safe Drinking Water Crisis among Low-income Urban Communities and Ways Forward”, organised by research organisation Barcik at the Mangrove Conference Hall in Satkhira town yesterday.
Satkhira Green Coalition President Abu Affan Roj Babu chaired the event, while municipal Water Supply Engineer Nimai Chandra Pal attended as the chief guest.
At the dialogue, Baddipur Colony residents Jahanara Khatun and Mariam Khatun said their neighbourhood remains waterlogged for nearly six months during the rainy season, causing an acute shortage of drinking water. Many households have yet to receive municipal water connections despite living within the city.
Professor Pabitra Mohan Das said he spends Tk1,600-1,700 a month buying jarred water for drinking and cooking. With an adequate municipal supply, the same needs could be met for around Tk200, he added.

item.title: 40 factories shut in Savar-Ashulia industrial belt amid labour unrest
item.description:
A group of workers gathered at Padmar Mor in Savar’s Hemayetpur around 3pm on Monday, briefly drawing attention to the area. Police later asked them to disperse peacefully, and they left the road shortly afterwards without further incident.
Meanwhile, around 40 factories remained closed in the Savar and Ashulia industrial areas on Monday, according to industrial police.
Of the closed factories, 27 were shut under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, while nine were declared closed indefinitely. The remaining factories were observing general holidays.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police (SP) of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, said workers at one factory refused to resume work after the lunch break and remained seated inside the premises. The factory authorities subsequently declared a holiday, he added.
Workers at two other factories also stopped working and remained seated, the SP said.
However, workers at other factories across the industrial areas continued their work peacefully, he added.

item.title: Icon Ronaldinho makes winning return to pro football in Italy's third division
item.description:
Greying and rounder in the face than during his prime, Ronaldinho made a winning return to professional football on Sunday for Ravenna, an ambitious club in Italy's third tier aiming to reach Serie A.
Under the watchful eye of Ignazio Cipriani, the Italian-American businessman who has owned the club since 2024, Ronaldinho perfectly played his role as the centrepiece of a clever PR stunt.
The 46-year-old Brazilian great put in a low-key performance in his first competitive match since playing for Fluminense in 2015, as Ravenna, bidding for promotion to Serie B, beat local rivals Forli 2-0 in front of a packed Stadio Bruno Benelli on Italy's Adriatic coast.
Known for his dynamic dribbling and often outrageous ball control in his heyday, Ronaldinho largely strolled around the pitch and laid off simple passes to his teammates, who would once upon a time not have been anywhere near his level as players.
Ronaldinho's arrival has given Ravenna a previously unimaginable profile, and Cipriani would no doubt have been delighted to see the pack of reporters and photographers that descended on the Benelli.
The 2005 Ballon d'Or winner only played in the first half but was involved in the move which ended with Giulio Donati smashing hosts Ravenna ahead in the 36th minute.
Ronaldinho entered the field to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Benelli having a temporary stand with 1,800 places -- dubbed "R10" -- added for the occasion.
Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli's "Con Te Partiro" blasting out of the stadium's speakers.
And he left after the first half, but not before plenty of handshakes with his teammates and match officials.
Only he knows whether he will play for Ravenna again, although he had only taken part in a single training session with his teammates before this one-off appearance.
He only arrived in Italy a few days before Sunday's match, suggesting that he hasn't committed himself for the long haul.
Ravenna, who have not even played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend's fixtures six points behind leaders Spezia.
One team for each of the three groups will be directly promoted to Serie B, with the final spot in the second tier decided.

item.title: Kroupi on target as France clinch Nations League quarters spot
item.description:
Eli Junior Kroupi scored his first France goal as Les Bleus beat Turkey 2-1 on Sunday to secure a spot in the quarter-finals of the UEFA Nations League.
France needed a draw in their last Group A1 outing to make sure of their progress to the quarter-finals next March, and they went ahead just after half-time in Bordeaux via an Emirhan Topcu own goal.
Bournemouth forward Kroupi, 20, replaced Bradley Barcola just past the hour and made it 2-0 from a Rayan Cherki assist, before Abdulkerim Bardakci pulled one back for Turkey at the death.
"At first I thought I was offside, but when I saw the goal had been given it was an incredible feeling," Kroupi, who has only just returned after missing the first two months of the season due to injury, told broadcaster TF1.
"Of course I was thinking about my injury. I hope I have left all that behind me and I can look forward now."
The result allowed Zinedine Zidane's French side to bounce back from a 3-1 loss away to Italy on Thursday as they finish on top of their group with 13 points, one point ahead of Belgium.
The Belgians also progress into the quarter-finals after coming from behind to thrash Italy 4-1 in Brussels.
France, who won the Nations League in 2021, are therefore guaranteed to play a runner-up from one of the other groups in League A in the quarters, the draw for which will take place this coming Friday.
World Cup winners Spain are among their potential opponents in the last eight.
"Our objective was to qualify, ideally in first place, so we have achieved our goal, but I was a bit perplexed with our performance," admitted Zidane.
"We rectified certain things at half-time, got our foot on the ball and were better in the second half, but there are things we still need to improve."
France have been hit by a host of injury issues, with last year's Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele among the many players missing for Zidane just now.
Captain Kylian Mbappe did return, however, after missing France's last four matches since scoring the winner in Turkey on Zidane's debut in September.
"I think he deserved to score a hat-trick today given the number of chances he had. I also liked the way he played without the ball. He played the role of captain marvellously," Zidane said of the Real Madrid superstar.
This game carried special significance for Zidane, who made his name as a player at Bordeaux in the 1990s before moving to Juventus and inspiring France to World Cup glory in 1998.
His return to the south-western city risked being spoiled by the performance of Turkey goalkeeper Berke Ozer, who frustrated France with a host of saves.
However, the home side went ahead in the 49th minute when Adrien Rabiot helped on a corner and Besiktas defender Topcu only succeeded in putting the ball over the line.
Kroupi, who scored 13 goals in the Premier League last season for Bournemouth, was handed a late call-up by Zidane after Marcus Thuram pulled out injured at the start of last week.
He won his first cap off the bench against Italy and notched his first France goal in the 80th minute here after combining superbly with Cherki.
That goal proved to be decisive as Bardakci replied in the 90th minute for Turkey, who finish with six defeats from six games.

item.title: Zverev too strong for debutant Jodar in ATP Finals
item.description:
World number one Alexander Zverev cruised through his opening match at the season-ending ATP Finals on Sunday, beating Spanish debutant Rafael Jodar 6–4, 6–4.
In the evening, American third seed Ben Shelton beat Frenchman Arthur Fils, seeded seventh, 6-2, 3-6, 6-3.
Zverev, who won the tournament in 2018 and 2021, needed just one hour and 27 minutes to overcome the season's breakout star.
Ranked 11th in the world, the 20-year-old Jodar is making his debut at the elite eight-player tournament.
Zverev had been eliminated in his opening match at the Paris Masters -- the final Masters 1000 event of the year -- and endured a lacklustre autumn as he blamed mental and physical exhaustion.
However, with 10 aces and a strong return of serve he stifled Jodar, who dropped his serve in the seventh game of the first set and again in the third game of the second.
"It wasn't the perfect match, but I'm happy; it's a great start to the tournament for me," Zverev said.
"With a 6-4, 6-4 win...against a Top 8 player in the world. You take that, for sure. I'm happy with the start, but I know I have to improve still."
In the other match in the John McEnroe group, Shelton secured his first-ever victory at the tournament. His debut appearance in 2025 ended with three defeats.
"It means a lot," Shelton said. "Especially doing it in the first match of the round robin, giving myself a little bit of momentum."
In the first set, Shelton overpowered Fils, the first Frenchman to qualify for the ATP Finals in 10 years.
The 22-year-old Fils then began to extend rallies. He forced his first break point of the match in eighth game and took it. He then saved two break points in the next game to tie the match.
Serving for the match in the final set, Shelton faced two break points but saved them with ferocious aces before pounding his way to the win with booming forehands.
"That was really intense, especially in the first set," Shelton said. "I don't know that I've played that many rallies out there on tour on a court this fast. So it was physical, really physical. A tough contest."
"I was breathing hard after pretty much every point, and I'm excited to get started in a match like that. Everything wasn't perfect, but my overall level was good and I thought it was a great match I will be able to build on this week."
He will face Zverev on Tuesday.
Zverev secured the world number one ranking in early November after winning his first two Grand Slam titles in 2026, but the 29-year-old is not necessarily the favourite in Turin.
Spaniard Carlos Alcaraz, ranked third in the world, who plays American Frances Tiafoe on Monday, is considered the favourite following his comeback from a wrist injury with three wins in five tournaments -- Tokyo, Vienna and the Paris Masters.
Italy's Jannik Sinner won the last two editions of the Finals but he has not played since winning Wimbledon in July due to a knee injury.

item.title: Andreeva defeats Svitolina to win WTA Finals
item.description:
Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva battled past Elina Svitolina in straight sets to win the season-ending WTA Finals crown on Sunday.
Andreeva powered to a 7-5, 6-3 victory in a hard-fought duel in Indian Wells to complete a superb week in California.
Reigning French Open champion Andreeva, 19, clinched the title without dropping a set in the tournament.
She is only the third teenager after Chris Evert and Maria Sharapova to win the WTA Finals on their debut.
"It feels amazing, of course I'm super-privileged to put my name in that group," said Andreeva.
The teenager thanked friends, family and support staff in a victory speech, before light-heartedly thanking herself for her success.
"I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work, for never quitting, for always believing in myself, for not taking the days off, for working every day, and for committing to what I have to do," said Andreeva, wearing a track-suit top with the slogan "I want to thank myself."
A grueling 1hr 48min duel saw Andreeva secure a break in the opening game of the first set before holding for a 2-0 lead.
Ukrainian veteran Svitolina broke back in the fourth game, conjuring a sublime angled volley to level at 2-2.
Svitolina was soon back under pressure though, conceding another break to go 4-3 down before Andreeva held for a 5-3 lead.
There was more drama to follow when Andreeva served for the first set at 5-4 up.
She opened with back-to-back double faults to go 0-30 down, and then yanked a wild forehand wide to give Svitolina two break points at 15-40.
A long forehand gave Svitolina the break to knot it at 5-5 but Andreeva hit back immediately with her third break of serve to regain the advantage at 6-5.
The Russian made no mistake when serving for the set for a second time, holding comfortably to go 1-0 up.
The second set followed a familiar pattern, with both players trading some brutal groundstrokes in a series of long rallies.
Andreeva broke to take the lead at 1-0 but Svitolina responded in a marathon second game, breaking back after converting her seventh break point to level at 1-1.
Andreeva edged back in front with a break to go 3-2 up and then held for a 4-2 lead.
The next two games went with serve to leave Svitolina serving to stay in the match at 5-3 down.
A fortunate net cord left Andreeva with three match points at 0-40.
Svitolina saved the first and looked poised to save another, only to hit a wide open overhead smash into the net to give Andreeva the win.
Svitolina, who had been thumped 6-4, 6-0 by Andreeva in the opening round-robin game of the tournament, took positives from her performance.
"After the first match I was not expecting to play in the final," Svitolina said. "Unfortunately it didn't go my way but I gave it my all."

item.title: Belgium smash Italy to reach Nations League quarters
item.description:
Belgium thumped Italy 4-1 to join France in the Nations League quarter-finals.
Sitting third in Group A1 ahead of kick-off and needing a win to qualify for the last eight, Belgium had their backs up against the wall when Francesco Pio Esposito volleyed Italy ahead in the 11th minute.
But Belgium blew Italy away in the following quarter of an hour, with Maxim De Cuyper and Nathan Ngoy bundling the hosts ahead before Jeremy Doku slalomed through the Azzurri defence and confidently shot home.
Mark van Bommel's team deservedly claimed a spot in the quarters and made sure the scoreline reflected the balance of play when one of many attacks against an open Italy defence ended with Diego Moreira slotting home with 10 minutes remaining.
A dismal night for Italy, who were top of the group after beating France last time out and just needed a draw to go through, was made even worse when Senne Lammens saved Esposito's weak late penalty.
"Nights like this can happen, unfortunately. These things can happen during a rebuilding process," said Italy boss Roberto Mancini.
"We're disappointed, but this is the kind of night that will ultimately prove useful to us."
France top the group after bouncing back from defeat to Italy with a 2-1 win over rock-bottom Turkey in Bordeaux.
Les Bleus will head into the draw for the last eight, scheduled for Friday in Nyon, Switzerland, as a seeded team, a position that ensures they will host the return leg in March 2027 but could mean they face Spain.
